subtopic: DEBATES-FIRST REPORT OF STANDINQ COMMITTEE

speechtext:
Mr. JEAN FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata) presented the first report of the standing committee on debates, as follows:
Your committee has given careful consideration to its order of reference under date of May 10, 1948, which reads as follows:
"That the advisability of continuing the publication of the revised edition of debates and the distribution of the unrevised edition of same, be referred to the said committee."
Your committee has heard Mr. Edmond Cloutier, King's Printer and Controller of Stationery, and Mr. Earl C. Young, Editor of Debates and Chief of Reporting Branch, House of Commons, and Mr. Yves Fortin, Production Supervisor of the Printing Bureau.
Your committee recommends:
1.	That the designations "unrevised" and "revised" editions be discontinued, and the day to day edition be known as the daily edition and the bound volume as the bound edition.
2.	That members be allowed eight calendar days, from the date on which the speech is made, to submit to the debates office necessary and permissible corrections in their speeches as reported in the daily edition, and that no corrections submitted after this period be accepted.
3.	That the pages of each daily edition be submitted to the printing bureau not later than nine days after the daily edition is published, and that once proofs of the corrected pages have been approved by the debates office they be assembled by the printing bureau for the bound edition.
4.	That the pages of the daily edition be kept intact so that, after permissible corrections are made, the pages of the daily edition can be used for the bound edition as originally printed, and that changes suggested by members be confined strictly to correction of errors and essential minor alterations.
5.	That effect be given forthwith to the recommendation contained in paragraph 4 above, for the present session and succeeding sessions.
6.	That no order for reprints of a member's speech be received by the debates office after the expiration of seven days from the date of the daily edition in which it appeared.
7.	That the distribution list of complimentary copies of debates allotted to members be hereinafter forwarded by the joint parliamentary distribution branch to the printing bureau for distribution.
Your committee further recommends that the government consider the advisability of increasing the number of complimentary copies of the daily edition of debates to members from 10 to 16.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
Jean Francois Pouliot,
Chairman

speechtext: Have steps been taken by the Bank of Canada to curtail the volume of new capital investment in Canada, and if so, what were they?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BANK OF CANADA-NEW CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Under existing conditions the volume of new capital investment in Canada is limited primarily by the available physical supply of labour, building materials and equipment rather than by monetary or financial policies. It is understood however that the Bank of Canada has expressed the view to the chartered banks that under today's conditions, when the rate of capital development is straining Canada's manpower and material resources, it is undesirable that funds required for the financing of capital expenditures should be obtained through an expansion of bank credit. The budget speech dealt in a general way with the economic and financial aspects of this question.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LEGISLATION TO BE INTRODUCED DURING THE PRESENT SESSION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LEGISLATION TO BE INTRODUCED DURING THE PRESENT SESSION
speechtext:
On Monday my hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) asked if I would give the house a statement of the legislation that is still to be brought down before the conclusion of the session. I need not make mention of measures that already appear on the order paper. They should however be kept in mind in reviewing the legislation that remains to be dealt with.
In the Votes and Proceedings of yesterday hon. members will see a notice of a resolution for the approval of the international wheat agreement. That resolution will appear on tomorrow's order paper. The following measures, as hon. members are aware, are being considered by committees of the house: an act to provide for the investigation, conciliation and settlement of industrial disputes; an act to amend the Loan Companies Act; an act to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1938; an act to amend the War Veterans' Allowance Act, 1946; an act to amend the Veterans' Insurance

Inquiries oj the Ministry
Act; an act to amend the Veterans' Rehabilitation Act. An act to amend the Yukon Placer Mining Act, and an act to amend the Yukon Quartz Mining Act are before a committee of the Senate. There will of course be the bills which arise out of the budget resolutions, and which include the following: a bill to amend the Income War Tax Act; a bill to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act; a bill to amend the Excise Tax Act; a bill to amend the Excise Act; a bill to amend the customs tariff.
Other measures to be introduced will include: a bill respecting Canadian National Railways financing and guarantee; re-introduction of the Income Tax Act; a bill to amend the Criminal Code; a bill to amend the Judges Act; a bill to amend the Lord's Day Act; a bill to amend the Government Annuities Act; a resolution and bill to amend the Yukon Act; a resolution and bill respecting the Northwest Territories commission; a bill to amend the Land Titles Act; a bill to amend the Manitoba Natural Resources Act; a bill to amend the Saskatchewan Natural Resources Act; a resolution and bill to amend the Diplomatic Service (Special) Superannuation Act; a bill to amend the Board of Transport Commissioners Act; bills respecting a tax convention between Canada and France and Canada and New Zealand; a bill to amend the National Battlefield Commission Act.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LEGISLATION TO BE INTRODUCED DURING THE PRESENT SESSION
speechtext: All by June 30.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LEGISLATION TO BE INTRODUCED DURING THE PRESENT SESSION
speechtext:
I think hon. members will find that most of these last-mentioned measures are relatively simple and non-controversial and may not occasion much in the way of discussion. I am not saying that the resolutions on the budget may not occasion debate. There are still a few more I should mention. These are possible measures. I do not say that they will be proceeded with, but perhaps it is just as well to take notice of them at once. Measures which may be introduced in the senate are: a bill to amend the Insurance Companies Act; a bill respecting the Quebec Savings Bank Act; a bill to amend the Bankruptcy Act.
Additional measures which may be introduced in this house are: a bill to amend the Exchequer Court Act; a bill to amend the Petition of Right Act; a bill to amend the Supreme Court Act; a bill to amend the Tariff Board Act; a bill to amend the Criminal Code (race meetings). I hope to introduce, and trust the house will receive its provisions favourably, a bill respecting the development of the national capital.
In addition to these measures there will be such legislation as may arise from reports of standing and select committees, in addition *to specific bills which have already been referred to them and further supplementary estimates. As always it is necessary to see things from as many sides as possible in advance. I should add that from time to time, measures may come forward, or may have to be brought forward, which are not thought of at the moment. I have not in mind any other measures being introduced. I do not wish to say that something may not arise between now and June 30 which may necessitate some further measure or measures being introduced.
As hon. members have just remarked, there are still but five weeks in which to complete this program, if that is to be done by the end of June. I hope that we may be able, among the parties themselves, so to organize business as to ensure the attainment of that end.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes-"hear, hear." I think that the mentality of the members of the opposition generally is all wrong in this matter of surpluses. In the United States of America there is a tradition with regard to surpluses which is different from ours. The belief there is that it is the duty of the government, not only in especially good times but in normal times, to effect a reduction of the national debt as rapidly as possible. From what I read in the weekly and monthly publications of the United States, I understand that pressure is put on the leaders by the membership of the house of representatives to make sure that all outgoings-not only current outgoings but loans and so on-are met out of operating revenues, and also that provision is made for progressive and rapid reduction in the national debt. That is done on a sound instinct; it is done on the instinct that guides prudent and successful people in their ordinary business enterprises.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would ask my hon. friend just to wait; I shall have a hard enough time, probably, before I get through.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are with you on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not want to have too many interruptions. But that is the tradition in the United States of America. I think we should attach more importance to that here. If we could have substantial surpluses over the next few years and reduce the national debt, it would make a great difference. Suppose we were able to reduce the debt by two and a half billion dollars. That would result in an interest saving of just under $70,000,000 a year, which would make it far easier for governments to meet the legitimate needs of the people. It is a crippling thing, and a defeatist attitude, to think that you must go on piling debts higher and higher on the ground that taxation of the people is plunder. The money, it must be understood, is not taken and divided among the cabinet ministers. The money is taken and applied to the reduction of the debt owed by the people of the country. From the standpoint of the man in the street, the ordinary people of the country, I think the policy of debt reduction, certainly in times like these, is a right policy.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews), who is a shrewd and experienced member of this house, the other night said this, as reported at page 4324 of Hansard:
I have no hesitation in saying that the minister has a sound idea in reducing our indebted-

ness each year to the largest possible degree now, when times -are good. You may call it cyclical budgeting, if you wish, but I call it plain common sense.
And plain common sense it is. Of course there is another important reason why extensive reductions in taxation should not take place at the present time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Let me quote from the budget speech as reported at page 4063 of Hansard:
What we do will affect the fortunes of our citizens and their cost of living. If we diverted our prospective surplus into a reduction of taxes now, it would add hundreds of millions of dollars a year to the already intense demands of Canadians for goods and services-but it would add nothing to the volume of Canadian goods and services -available for sale. People would try to buy more, but there would not be more to buy, unless the effort to get it resulted in more imports that we cannot afford and which we would have to shut out somehow or other. Prices would be sure to rise. Some people would profit, but others would lose out to the higher cost of living. The apparent benefits of tax reduction would prove to be a mirage except to those strong or fortunate groups which can profit more -than they suffer by higher prices.
And later on:
Now is the time to lay the foundation for employment budgets in future, while fighting inflation at present.
I would commend that sentence to the judgment and consideration of the members of this house.
There is another consideration that I think ought to be placed before the house. Our income tax level now, on the average, is lower than that of the United States of America. The United States of America is taking dramatic steps for assistance in European recovery. If we in this country had a stock of United States exchange, I presume that we would be doing what we have done consistently in the past-that is, we would doubtless be assisting by the extension of credits for European recovery, because we have such a heavy stake in European recovery. But we cannot do that, or we cannot do it to any appreciable extent, because of our exchange position. On the other hand, we shall be supplying goods. Undoubtedly there will be large offshore purchases, as they are called, from Canada under the European recovery plan being administered by the United States of America. But it would be undesirable, I feel sure, having in

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley
mind public opinion in the United States, to have a situation arise such as this: that the people of the United States should be keeping their taxes up to the high levels they have now attained, and that Canada, not contributing toward European recovery by way of credits, should seize the opportunity to push her taxes down and cash in on the situation in such a way that we would inevitably be severely criticized and penalized by others.
I come now to the main part of the speech that I rose to make. I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) on Friday evening. He said two or three things in his speech that I want to use more or less as a text. They are good principles. He said that what we needed-I am not quoting him verbatim, but just giving the effect of his words-in considering these matters is realism, clear thinking, and intellectual honesty. I want to apply those tests to some of the criticisms that have been made of the government's financial policy, and to some of the positions that have been taken by the opposition.
To begin with, I submit that if the hon. gentleman had applied those tests to one instance he gave, he would not have given it. On Friday afternoon he told the house that the taxation on the average Canadian family of five was something over $1,300, and he arrived at that figure by taking the per capita taxation in Canada and multiplying it by five. That is one place where the multiplication table just does not apply. A family of five usually includes two or three young children; and to take the average per capita taxation, all the money raised from the rich and the poor, from corporations and from individuals, and get a per capita amount and then say the average family of five is paying five times as much as the average individual in Canada, is a gross fallacy and should not have been used by an hon. member ordinarily as careful as the financial critic of the opposition.
The budget speech strikes me as having those qualities outlined by the hon. gentleman-of realism, clearness of thought, intellectual honesty and recognition of the facts; and I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) not only on recognizing those facts but on his devotion to duty in acting accordingly. He knew he would run into a barrage of unreasonable, demagogic opposition criticism, but he did what he knew he ought to do. He defended his decision in a budget speech of unanswerable logic. His course of action will be approved by large numbers of Canadians today, but, more
important still, it will be approved by all Canadians in the years to come.
As I said at the outset, the statement has been made that our action in restoring the Canadian dollar to par in terms of United States dollars on July 5, 1946, was the sole cause, or at least the chief cause, of our loss of United States dollars in 1947, and was thus indirectly the reason for the restrictions introduced last fall. Some of those who take that position work themselves up to a high pitch of assurance indeed. For instance, the other evening the hon. member for Eglinton said:
We have had a sample of it in this country since the great blunder-
Everything is either "plunder" or "blunder".
-the great blunder in the middle of 1946 and the constant flight of United States dollars from Canada ever since, a flight and a policy which almost brought this country to economic ruin in 1947.
Well, the responsible critics do not go that far, but some of them do say this was one of the greatest mistakes in our financial history. I should like to reply to this charge, because I regard it as entirely unfounded.
Let us recall the situation. The revaluation of our dollar was part of our policy of price control. On July 5, 1946, I recommended that four steps be taken: first, that the price ceiling be changed from a general to a specific basis; second, that subsidies be continued where needed to continue price control; third, that price ceilings on imports be set not on a fixed price but on an imported cost plus a limited mark-up basis; and fourth, that the Canadian dollar be raised to par with the United States dollar.
Four days earlier, on July 1, 1946, price control in the United States had lapsed or collapsed; it had ended, and the step here in Canada was taken having in mind that fact among others. We took the step we did for several reasons. First, we knew that sooner or later there would be an inevitable adjustment of our prices to United States prices. We could not see any reason why, by keeping our dollar ten per cent below the United States dollar, we should inflict upon our people permanently a cost level and price level ten per cent higher than that of the United States. In the second place, we were making heavy loans to Great Britain, and the revaluation of our dollar would encourage imports from Great Britain and reduce the necessity of credits. Third, our whole policy of price control was gradual decontrol, not sudden decontrol as in the United States; and if price control was to be retained and eased off by
The Budget-Mr. Ilsley

stages, as was done subsequently and I am sure wisely done, a step of this kind would be of great assistance.
Few policies of a Canadian government ever received such general acceptance. The opposition took no exception to that policy. There was some suggestion that we should have done it in two stages instead of one; that is, five per cent then and later another five per cent, but we replied to those criticisms at the time. The opposition took no exception to bringing our dollar back to par. To listen to them here one would think they had opposed the step. They did nothing of the kind, nor did the public at large. One has only to look at the newspaper headlines of the day to see the widespread approval that was given. It was not until much later that any volume of criticism developed. This was based on hindsight, not on foresight; but as I shall now show, it is not valid criticism even now. The hindsight on which it is based makes a false appraisal of causes and effects.
The first statement made is that the step we took unduly encouraged imports from the United States and discouraged exports to that country. First I shall deal with the imports. There is no doubt that there has been a large increase in the volume of imports from the United States, though apparently the peak has been passed. The financial critic of the opposition stopped at February; he did not go on to March, and of course he had not the figures for April. When we recall that this increase in the volume of imports from the United States has taken place in the face of a forty per cent increase in United States prices, surely it is unreasonable to think another ten per cent would have made any difference, or certainly much of a difference. One of the main reasons why Canadian importers were bringing in so much from the United States was that prices were going up in the United States, and they thought the time to buy was before prices went up further. But there were other reasons. Half our two billion dollars' worth of imports from the United States are essentials we have to import, regardless of the exchange rate. Imports of such commodities as coal, steel, cotton and manufacturing components come in anyway-when production is at a high level in Canada. The volume of these imports rises when our production rises and falls when our production falls, regardless of the exchange rate. The cost of such imports is only a part, and often a small part, of the cost of production or the cost of capital expansion; and a mere ten per cent on the price of such imports would have no effect whatever on their volume.
fMr. Ilsley.]
It has been estimated that not more than twenty-five per cent of Canada's imports from the United States are consumer goods. Here the volume of imports would be more sensitive to price; but even in this field the purchasing power of the Canadian consumer has been so great during this period that in all probability the revaluation of the dollar has had no appreciable effect on volume. But while the volume of imports from the United States was affected, if at all, only to a negligible extent by the revaluation, the importation from overseas was much more sensitive. Prices of European goods were very high by Canadian standards, and many of them were consumer goods that could hardly be classed as essentials. The demand for these goods is very responsive to price - changes. Whatever was the proper policy with reference to imports from the United States, there can be no doubt about one thing: we want to encourage importations from overseas countries, and the revaluation of the dollar worked in that direction.
Some irresponsible statements have been made about the extent to which the imports were increased by the revaluation. I am glad however to note that the financial critic of the opposition has ceased emphasizing this feature of the revaluation-he did in his speech last Friday at any rate-and seems to be concentrating entirely upon its effect on the import of capital, about which I shall speak in a few moments.
I come now to our exports. So far as I can ascertain, the revaluation has had no effect in diminishing our exports. One can imagine conditions when depreciation of our dollar would encourage exports by giving us a better competitive position in foreign markets. But in conditions of today, with our costs of production such as they are and our exchange rate at its present level, our exporters are able to sell on a competitive basis in any of the markets of the world. So here the argument against revaluation falls down completely.
Even in the tourist industry, which is economically a species of export, there is no evidence at all that the revaluation has diminished the flow of tourists to this country or that a devaluation would increase it. The cost of vacations in Canada is, in all probability, lower than the cost of vacations in the United States; tourists from the United States obtain many of their dollars from the unofficial market anyway; they are quite free to obtain Canadian funds from the unofficial market, and there is nothing in the figures to indicate

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley
that the revaluation effected any slowing down of tourist movements into this country.
The only export industry upon which the revaluation admittedly had some effect was the gold mining industry. It was recognized from the start that this industry, by its very nature an anticyclical industry, would be adversely affected to some extent, and compensatory measures have accordingly been adopted. A careful, well-reasoned estimate made by a writer in Toronto Saturday Night placed the probable increase in exports of gold to the United States under a ninety-cent Canadian dollar over the exports of gold under a hundred-cent Canadian dollar at not more than 815,000,000 a year. But there were other export industries which used the revaluation as the occasion for increasing their prices. This is the reason I said there was no ascertainable net effect in diminishing or discouraging exports from Canada to the United States or to other hard currency countries.
I understand that Premier Drew placed the figure I have just given as $15,000,000 at 8100 million a year, but without any facts whatever to support his figure, which, in my judgment, is a completely wild one. Taking the imports and exports together, therefore, everything indicates that the revaluation had nothing but a negligible effect on our balance of payments with the United States on current operations- that is, when we consider exports and imports together, the whole situation.
Now, let us look at the effect it had on capital movements. It is on this point that the financial critic of the opposition speaks with immense assurance. This is what he said in his speech last Friday at pages 4244 and 4245:
The second result was the measure taken then to cut off American investment, practically like turning a tap. It has been a natural and, I submit, inevitable and useful part of the economic structure of the country from the outset that we should have American investment, and free American investment . . . That was cut off . . . It does seem an irony. In the first six months of 1946 nature was beginning to take its course. We were receiving American investments at the rate of $25,000,000' a month, which was very useful, and then we cut them off . . . American investments in this country are out of balance, as I said a moment .ago. They are natural to us, and we cannot go on importing as we are now unless the Americans will again invest.
Let us look at the kind of investment that was being made by Americans in Canada prior to revaluation. Most of it was the speculative purchase of Canadian securities-many of them government securities. Americans were buying these securities believing that our dollar was valued too low and that it would
inevitably have to be revalued. The investment was the purchase of existing securities- securities either of governments or of existing enterprises; and most of it was a purchase for speculative reasons. This is not the kind of investment that we really welcome. Indeed, for years I used to worry when I learned of increasing speculative American purchases of our securities. I realized that we were simply running into debt to a foreign country, placing a mortgage, as it were, upon our own resources to residents of the United States-a mortgage that was sure to be called at some uncertain and unfavourable time when the holders of the securities decided to sell them.
To hear the financial critic of the opposition one would think that the kind of investment that the revaluation discouraged was the investment of risk capital, the kind of capital that develops new enterprises, the kind of investment which we welcome. But this was not for the most part the kind of investment that was being made, nor was there anything in the revaluation to discourage that beneficial type of investment. Investors of risk capital have been able throughout to obtain Canadian dollars in the unofficial market, indeed for most of the period at around 90, the very price to which we are told we should reduce our dollar.
If anyone were to ask my personal opinion as to why risk capital did not come in last year, I would say it was because of the repeated rumours that have been circulated that the Canadian dollar was to be devalued to 90 cents, or lower if necessary, a course which has been advocated in the house by members of the official opposition. It is not that kind of prospect, but exchange stability, that investors of risk capital have been seeking; and I am glad to say that we have begun in recent months to see confidence returning in our exchange and an increasing volume of risk capital being invested in this country.
When the financial critic says that we could go on importing if we could go on borrowing American money, this is true. But to go on basing our imports on great and ever greater borrowing from abroad would not be a desirable development.

speechtext: What about investments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To employ a term used by the financial critic, it would be living off our fat and doing so with a vengeance-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not if it were investments.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
-and paving the way for serious trouble in the future. Even if it were
The Budget-Mr. Ilsley

desirable, devaluation now would not cause the 1945-46 type of investment to be resumed, because the expectation of another appreciation of our dollar would be absent.
Then it is said there should be some devaluation. The opposition has been confused in its advocacy of devaluation. There has been a tendency on the part of some members, notably the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), to talk as if the Canadian dollar should be free, should be allowed to find its own level; but this view is not general, and for very good reasons. The financial critic has never been bold enough to go this far. He has been selecting 90 cents as the proper level. Why 90 cents rather than 95, or 85 or 80, nobody knows; but 90 cents it is, so far as he is concerned. I am glad to note, however, that in his speech on the budget he has not resumed his advocacy of a depreciation to 90 cents. I do not know whether there is some opposition policy other than the one he has just stated. Indeed he did not in his speech advocate any depreciation. However, the last opposition policy to be stated in the house is devaluation to 90 cents.
Now, everything I have said indicates that a devaluation to 90 cents would have no significant effect so far as curtailment of the volume of American imports is concerned, no significant effect on increase in the volume of Canadian exports, and no effect whatever on increase in the volume of desirable American investments in Canada. Its only certain effect would be an unfortunate increase in the Canadian price level, and an almost certain reduction in imports from the United Kingdom and other overseas countries. Surely such a policy has nothing to commend it.
It is also said that the true value of our dollar is indicated by the value of Canadian dollars in the unofficial markets in the United States. Nothing could be more fallacious than this allegation. The unofficial market in the United States is in no real sense a market in Canadian dollars.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How can the minister say that? He has just referred to investments through the unofficial market.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But it is not an indication of the true value of the Canadian dollar.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If hon. gentlemen will please hold their peace I will tell them in a moment. It is merely a market in limited-use Canadian dollars. The Canadian dollars that are sold in the unofficial market in the United States can be used only for a severely limited number of

purposes. They can be used by tourists in Canada; they can be used for capital investment in Canada, but they cannot be used for the great bulk of ordinary commercial transactions, such as payment for goods and services, freight charges, interest on dividends, or to settle any other current payments owing to Canadians. The official rate is rising at the present time. The resoluteness with which we are setting our exchange position in order is creating a growing demand in the unofficial market in the United States for these limited-use Canadian dollars, but that market is no indication of the true value of the Canadian dollar and no guide whatever to what the natural or proper rate ought to be.
The financial critic of the opposition said last Friday, as reported at page 4246 of Hansard:
To me a convincing argument and one that outweighs all others is the appeal to realism. When you find things happening between people who are trading with each other freely, that comes as close to realism as you can get. To me it is not real for us here in Canada to sit in an ivory tower saying our dollar is worth one hundred American cents when actually it is being traded in the United States at between 92 and 93 cents. We too much resemble King Canute.
When the hon. gentleman says this he is violating the principles which he laid down in his own speech-those of clear thinking and realism. He is using an argument which is specious; he is spreading a fallacy; he is misleading the public.
It is said that had we not taken this step there would have been no need for the November restrictions.
If what I have said is correct, it will be seen that the restrictions would have been necessary whether or not we had taken the step of July 5, 1946. The perpetuation of a cheap Canadian dollar would not have stopped our loss of exchange to the United States, probably not to any extent at all, and certainly not more than to a very minor extent. The proper policy to restore our exchange position was a policy which, while not discriminatory, was discriminating-that is, inviting and encouraging the imports we wanted, and excluding the imports we did not want; a policy which accomplishes the ends really desired, not many other ends which are thoroughly undesirable, such as raising the Canadian price level, discouraging imports from the United Kingdom, and the others I have mentioned.
It was said by the member for Muskoka-Ontario, quite inexcusably, that since the adoption of the present restrictions our present position in United States dollars shows little or no improvement over the low point of last

The Budget-Mr. Church
December. His authority for this statement is, he says, the Ottawa correspondent of Maclean's magazine, whose bald statement he takes in preference to the figures given by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. When Canadians realize that our holdings of hard currency exchange sank rapidly and steadily all through 1947 to a low of $461 million on December 16 last, and that by the end of April, 1948, they have climbed again to $588 million, apart altogether from what we have borrowed from the Export-Import bank, they will see not only that the downward trend has been arrested, but that an upward trend has been substituted for it and that our position is righting itself. How, then, can he say that the policy of November 1947 has failed? We have every reason to be gratified by the results of that policy.
I believe, for the reasons I have given, that our revaluation policy was sound at the time we adopted it, and that it continues to be sound today.

I believe it is a fact that no less a person than the governor of the Bank of Canada pointed out that while for the moment there is apparently a rise-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have always had a great respect for the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott); I have admired his urbanity and the way in which he has treated members who are not on his side of the house. I wish to point out one or two things concerning the policy of the government and the brain trust back of the government, although I wish it to be understood that I am not criticizing officials,
because, after all is said and done, matters of policy in the end are decided by the government itself.
Hon. gentlemen opposite were very largely to blame for the scuttling of the British empire by the policy they adopted at Bretton Woods, followed by the United States loan agreement, which have proved most disastrous to the cause of the empire and of Great Britain.
We also know what happened at the Geneva trade conference in February last year. For eight months we could get no information about what was going on at Geneva in the making of trade pacts over the head of the House of Commons while parliament was in session. Then in October or November our delegates came back and the government inaugurated their austerity program, which pretty nearly wrecked this country and the empire. Parliament was called for December 5.
I wish to refer to some government policies which are most unfair to Ontario and Quebec, which are paying over seventy per cent of the cash taxes of this country. The government took away their sources of revenue, and that, as well as the heavy burden of taxation from which we are suffering, has caused a great deal of unrest.
I wish we had the municipal system in vogue in this parliament. Our system of responsible government, which in my opinion, is not responsible government at all, is one hundred and fifty years old. If we had the more modern municipal system the estimates could be considered by the minister, the chief officials and certain members from all parties in the house, who could strike off certain expenditures. There is no reason why this country, years after the close of the war, should be spending money like water over the head of parliament. We have been too extravagant. Economy is not wanted. Parliament never hears of the expenditures until it conducts a post mortem on the estimates and after interim supply has been granted for nearly nine months. This parliament knows practically nothing of the action taken.
The budget address is probably the last time that a private member has a chance to say anything about world conditions and what is going on in this country. I contend that if we had the municipal system it would give the committee the right to revise proposed expenditures, because the present policies of the government are very largely wrong. We need some system of checks and balances in relation to expenditures. If the municipalities used the system we use in this house they
The Budget-Mr. Church

would all go bankrupt, but they are bound by the Municipal Act. The Municipal Act does not give them power to spend money like water as the government of the day is doing. Sections of the Municipal Act provide that none of these charges can be made except on a year-to-year basis, and in certain cases money bylaws for capital expenditure have to be voted on by the people.
If the government are sincere about the present budget they should hold an election. I believe that the election has been delayed for some time to come. I say that this budget was very largely made at Washington. We have those periodical excursions all over the seven seas. Our ambassadors and financiers are making these excursions. Donald Gordon has recently been issuing statements across the border. Then we have those conferences all over the world. For a month now we have had green grass and flowers, and the birds have been congregating and chattering. So do we in conferences; the same applies to our delegates and financiers and all the rest of them. They are on the seven seas. We are now having conferences. We are a nation of conferences. One mistake we made was in surrendering to Washington too much political, military, economic, financial and social initiative. This is nothing but a Washington-made budget over the head of parliament, following out what was done at Geneva away back in February 1947.
If we look closely at the budget we shall see that it is nothing but window-dressing, preparing for an election. What has become of the old Liberal doctrine of the people ruling in the country? The people do not rule. Now we have a family compact. Who controls the family compact? The brain trusts and the officials who give this advice. As I said the other day, there is an old Scotch proverb which says, when you go away up in the clouds be sure you keep one foot on the ground. We have no such thing as that here. It was referred to by me the other day on the amendment of the minister to abolish the penny bank.
There is no such thing as thrift in this country today. The government do not appreciate thrift because they bring in these astronomical figures running into billions and billions of dollars. In the civil estimates they are spending nearly $2 billion; whereas in 1896 the Tupper government spent $36,000,000, and the population has gone up only one-fourth since. Before the war the government spent $400 million on civil estimates; today it is up to $2 billion, with-
[ Mr. Church.]
out any control over the expenditures; so much so that interim supply is passed for about nine months of the year, and over the head of parliament, and we cannot strike off one dollar. I am opposed to this principle. What has become of the principle of government by the people, of the people and for the people? It does not exist in Canada today. The executive rule the land from coast to coast. They bring in a budget and the whole House of Commons has to swallow it. You cannot strike off a dollar. If you do, the government is defeated and must resign.
If we had the municipal system here we would be able to strike off from one-third to one-half the present cost of civil government in Canada, and give the people back home in the constituencies a chance. Mr. Fielding and Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that the sales tax should never go above a maximum of four per cent. It went to six, then to eight. They did cut it to four on food; it should come down to two. The reduction should apply not only to food, but to clothing and all the necessities of life.
If the budget is what the minister, the financiers and the government say it is, then the government should hold an election on it. If it is a popular budget, the government should go to the country on it. It should be decided by the electors. Why is the government afraid to hold an election in Canada and get the verdict of the people on it? I tell the house that it is a blessing that Ontario and Quebec did not adopt the Sirois report. It is the most mischievous report I have ever read. It is taxation without representation. We pass interim supply without any information. This system of taking such huge sums of money, nearly a billion dollars above what we need in 1948, is wrong. We are taking too much money out of the pockets of the taxpayers.
The minister says that such a policy will save us from inflation. Have hon. members ever heard of such a ridiculous doctrine? I do not know where it was invented. I can tell you that this system of taking all that money out of the workingman's pocket and using it for the purposes indicated, more than the minister needs, is against the principle of the Municipal Act, which requires expenditures to run only from year to year. By this system we are creating inflation. This system of budgeting amounts to putting your hands in the workingman's pockets until there is nothing left, particularly when we remember that taxation is very high, and the high cost of living is added on to it. Not enough has been charged to capital. Too much has been charged to pay-as-you-go.

The Budget-Mr. Church
This generation is suffering in flesh and blood. Why should the sins of the who-le human race be carried by this generation of people in Canada? A large part of the present budget should be charged to capital and not to income, because there is no income to justify it. There is no retrenchment, and no attempt at reduction of taxation. It makes the poor people back in the constituencies wonder what the House of Commons is for. The executive over our heads can pass a budget like this, and nine months of supply, without any real discussion at all of any of the individual items of the estimates. We find no retrenchment at all, but sky-high extravagance in every department of the public service.
No attempt is made to reduce taxation. The reduction of taxation is held in contempt by the various departments. You have only to look at the estimates to find that out. The poor working classes had hoped that at this session they would receive a reduction in the high income tax. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) the other day referred to the working classes and the small income tax payer. A reduction in these high taxes is badly needed by this class of people. In Britain they have reduced the income tax. In that country two million people do not now pay income taxes at all. The minister in his budget made a comparison with taxes in the United States and Britain, and published two tables. His comparison was most unfair, because there are many differences. As a result of the policies which hon. gentlemen opposite have put into effect, a person today, if he wishes to exist at all, has to utilize what little saving he has put by or any little money investment he may have.
Last year the house had not much opportunity to discuss the main or supplementary estimates. As I pointed out when we voted interim supply last month, while it is true that the minister must have money to run the services of the country, businessmen, retail merchants and others have been looking for retrenchment in government expenditures. Practically all we are doing now in committee of supply is holding a post mortem after the money is spent. That is no way to conduct the business of the country.
The government are spending money like water. I can see no sign of retrenchment in the main estimates or in the supplementaries. We are being asked to vote large sums of money for bonuses, subventions and subsidies for the prairie provinces, and the other provinces do not get anything. There are many items here for interim supply, one for S80 million, another for $17 million, and so on. These expenditures, under this method of conducting
the business of the country, really mean expenditures and taxation without representation. The house is abdicating its functions to the executive. It is a dangerous principle. Expenditures for civil government in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier amounted in 1897 to $36 million, and the population of the country has increased by only one-third or one-quarter since; but the civil estimates are now nearly two billions.
There should be some better way of conducting public business. The municipalities would be bankrupt if they did business in this way. The auditor general should have wider powers to deal with some of these expenditures. The Minister of Finance may take this humorously, but it is no laughing matter for the working classes I represent. Government extravagance and lack of retrenchment, added to the high cost of living, are becoming scandalous, and the public will not stand for it. We should have some redress of grievances before the executive spend money in this way by interim supply.
I have referred to the sales tax. Who pays the income tax? Taxation, so far as the industrial workers are concerned, is levied at the source? But what about the rest of the community? I am not here to criticize any particular class, and I do not mind saying that I have a great admiration for the farmers; but according to the figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics, for the last year of record, there were 705,973 farms in the country and only a small percentage of the farmers filed any income tax returns. The total cash income of farmers, reported by the bureau of statistics, in 1946 was $1,769,632,000, and it went over the two billion dollar mark last year. The bureau explains that farm cash income does not include income accruing to farmers from outside sources, nor does it include the value of products consumed in the farm home.
Who are the people who are prosecuted in our courts for offences in connection with income tax? I can find no farmers being prosecuted for violations of the act. And so far as the other offences are concerned, in connection with controls, for example, the people who are prosecuted are those who live in the cities. One druggist in the city of Montreal was fined only five dollars for giving out as an aid to his business pounds of butter. There should be some uniform, reciprocal system about prosecutions for all, not for some. I have always maintained that the principle of confederation for us to observe should be "each for all and all for each", because I do not believe in having legislation that does not apply to all classes
The Budget-Mr. Church

of citizens. Prosecution should be impartial, and not just for industrial workers; but this is not so.
The official opposition in this house have been urging economy in government, but without any success. Take the main estimates for this year and you will find they are sky-high in eveiy department of the public service. People have no idea where the money will come from. The opposition have done their duty by trying to point out where economies could be effected, but the government goes on spending freely.
One matter to which I would call the attention of the house is the practice of nonresidents of coming into Ontario and taking part in provincial elections. Outsiders from other provinces are coming in, visiting provincial constituencies and making speeches. I have never taken part in any election held in any other province, either in the maritimes, on the prairies or in British Columbia, but I find, in almost every newspaper I pick up, reports indicating that some of my hon. friends to the left have been going around Ontario addressing meetings. I am not questioning their right to do so, but I have always taken the view that it is not the right thing for anyone to go into another province and take part in provincial or municipal elections, unless he is a ratepayer there also.
I listened the other day to my hon. friend the member of Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), for whom I have a great deal of respect, discussing conditions in the maritime provinces, especially in connection with hydro-electric power. May I point out to hon. members that in the operation of our hydro-electric development in Ontario for cheap light and power we never receive one dollar by way of grant from the federal treasury. I object, therefore, to paying a third of the cost of steam plants or anything of that kind in other provinces.
What we need in Canada is a sound protectionist policy of bonuses, subventions and subsidies to solve the economic problems of each province. How has development been brought about in Ontario? The industrial development by the use of electrical equipment in Toronto, Brantford and other cities in the province has been the result of a policy of protection, and we have done a great deal under the British preferential agreements and the Ottawa agreements, requiring United States industrial institutions to have plants in Canada. But hon. gentlemen opposite, with one wave of the hand, by means of Bretton Woods, the American loan,

and the notorious Geneva undertaking, have destroyed all the great preferential trade of empire.
Why can we not have preferential trade within the empire? This government, through its free trade policies, has made it difficult for Canadian industry to carry on. Take the agricultural implement industry. Through the protectionist policy, that industry was built up in Canada, giving work to thousands of our people. The Massey-Harris Company, for instance, provided employment for a great many of our fellow Canadians, but the policy of this government has endangered that industry. There would not be an industry left in Canada if the government had its way, and the industrial provinces will pay for it in the years to come. I do not believe in the free trade doctrine, with all this wave of internationalism.
In my opinion the maritime provinces are largely to blame for the condition in which they find themselves at the present time, under their free trade theories. They moved certain head offices to Montreal. With their rich resources and their supply of coal they could have developed industries, and they cannot now expect to rap at the door of the dominion and claim bonuses, subventions and subsidies toward their power development. I introduced a bill in 1923 for the establishment of a national fuel policy, and I received little support from the maritimes except from the late Senator Logan and the present Hon. Mr. Justice Carroll.
As regards immigration, I agree with the views put forward by the Canadian Legion in their meeting at Saskatoon yesterday when they called for more British immigration. We have now taken our fair share of the displaced persons, and something should be done immediately. Otherwise the cream of immigration will go from the British isles to Australia and New Zealand where they are welcomed. The governments there are welcoming large bodies of British people, our own kith and kin, who saved our shores in the last war, with only the aid of the dominions, and, two years later, with the help of our devoted allies to the south. Immigration from the British isles should receive more attention, and there should be mass immigration from there now as there is to Australia.
As I said recently, what are we going to do about Newfoundland when the election takes place on June 3? I dealt with this matter away back last year in connection with the Labrador bill. I believe that the doctrine should be taken up actively by Britain and by Canada, namely, that of lease-lend by which all the bases were given up from Newfoundland right down to British Guiana. That lease

The Budget-Mr. Church
should be cancelled now once and forever. It is a 99-year lease, practically a freehold. It was done to aid America in the battle of the Atlantic against invasion. That lease should be cancelled and should be charged up to lease-lend. Newfoundland will not be talked out of the empire any more than Canada will be. Newfoundland will have to be fought out of the empire.
I have never known a time equal to the last four years when, as Mr. Churchill says, more effort has been made to scuttle the empire and liquidate it. That effort has been made not only in India, but in the Suez, Egypt, Palestine, with the loss of the Mediterranean lifeline, and in many other parts of the world where that policy has been carried on. Britain will not sit down and be content to be a second-class power and allow dollar statesmanship to cripple her forever. She still rules the waves and "Britons never shall be slaves" as James Thomson, the great Scotch poet said, when he wrote "Rule Britannia" at the time of the Spanish Armada.
A retired United States admiral said recently that the United States has now taken Britain's place and rules the waves. That was not so at Pearl Harbor. I am against Britain being a second-class power, notwithstanding all that is said and done. I am opposed to any more scuttling of our empire. Many things looked impossible. The mother country kept world peace and security for centuries against dictators-against Philip of Spain, Louis XIY, Napoleon and twice in our own generation against the Kaiser and Hitler of Germany. Next to the Christian church no other agency has done as much for the freedom of the world and for liberty and civilization as the mother country has done on the seven seas. Did not the battle of Britain in the last war look impossible? Everything looked impossible including the battle of the Atlantic, as did the exploits of Drake, Raleigh, Nelson, Blake and others. The mother country, notwithstanding the terms of the Bretton Woods agreement and the hard terms of the United States loan, can live a few more months the hard way. We see the utter collapse of statesmanship in America and also in this Geneva dollar pact proposition.
As I said the other day regarding Canada, it has never had a foreign policy. The foreign policy of Canada is "We have no commitments; parliament will decide." Our foreign policy is to be linked up with the United States. I am a great admirer of the people of the United States, and of what they did. It was of the utmost importance. We should have the most friendly relations with them
because, with Britain and the dominions, they are the hope of the world. There should be the most friendly relations between Britain, the dominions and the United States.
We are now making the same mistake again. We are trying by the UNO to appease Russia and are adopting an appeasement policy. She does not want it and she refuses it. The United States did not have a foreign policy until recently when they adopted the ERP, Mr. Marshall's program, which has not yet been put into effect to any great extent, although it is now getting beyond the blueprint stage. However I will say this. The policy which they are now pursuing is on again, off again and on again, and all that kind of thing. That country decides one thing about Palestine and marches up the hill today politically, then tomorrow marches down the hill for the sake of safety as a nation as it sees the partition difficulty. That is meant for local consumption in the coming election as well.
The committee on foreign affairs, which has been meeting recently, and whose appointment I opposed, is one of the most mischievous committees we ever had. One has just to read the papers of the last few days to find out what they are saying down there. They have government officials before them. What are the government officials doing? They are deciding the foreign policy of the government themselves in these matters, over the heads of the House of Commons, while we are in session. Did you ever hear of such functions in a committee on foreign affairs? They want more embassies on the seven seas. As I said the other night, if UNO at Lake Success were only to close down for a year, we might have some hope for peace. Our parliamentary association turned itself into a pan-American association. It forgets all about the empire and goes on thinking, as Time magazine said recently, that we are becatning, in an economic way, the 49th state in the union. As I said, the officials should not be laying down these foreign policies of their own volition over the head of parliament now in session.
Then there is the matter of extravagance of the various departments. For instance, let us take the Department of External Affairs. They have ambassadors and embassies on the seven seas, consuls and consuls-general. There are trade commissioners, but these are useful in obtaining trade. A big trade conference is opening next Saturday in Toronto. I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and many members of the house will go there to see what can be done. Having all these officials overseas is useless duplication. The trade commissioners do fine work; but why
The Budget-Mr. Church

should we have carloads of these other ambassadors on the seven seas? Most of them are not ambassadors; they know nothing at all about diplomacy, except what they learn by experience. We have various ones going around the seven seas making speeches along these lines as well, and the empire is being scuttled accordingly.
I can say this about economy. It is talked of by all the ministers when they speak. The Minister of Finance has been comparing his budget with that of Britain and the United States. Economy is talked of by all the ministers, but that is only for us. Economy is the last thing the minister thinks of, because he has his experts, secretaries, first secretary, second secretary-they are copying the external affairs department-third secretary, fourth secretary, fifth secretary; and where do the public come in while all this is going on? This matter of economy is the last thing the ministers think of. It is not for them to practise. The public must save, or where would the money come from for ministers to spend? We have been told that over and over again. Where would the money come from for the ministers to spend if the people did not save?
The greatest wheeze, as a writer says, is the newly invented economic doctrine and theory, solemnly supported by a lot of honest deputies, no doubt, but who misjudged the situation. What they say is their policy is made by the brain-trusters and others. They are all good men, and some of them should know better than to swallow all this and make it a political budget instead of a financial and economic one, and make the public pay this vast taxation as a remedy against inflation. They say that for the Minister of Finance to collect several hundred million dollars more than he requires will, in some mysterious way, make for a sounder economy. But I cannot find that in any of the modem textbooks. The only way to get back to a sound economy would be for the minister to cut the coat according to the cloth and to stop the huge waste now going on on the seven seas. We can only do that if the minister takes a strong stand, and if we stop borrowing from foreign countries. My principle has always been to tell the people the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, but that is not what is done in this budget. The government should not be afraid to tell the people they have made a mistake, and should never have a budget that legislates against human nature as this one does.
On April 6 the budget was brought down in the old country. The National Review says it was a political budget of Sir Stafford Cripps, containing little to hearten the people of the mother country in the face of the austerity

now prevailing there. The keynotes are dependence upon America; that they must continue to lavish public money on socialist projects, and that this money must be obtained from the enterprising and thrifty. It is the old story of taking money in excessive amounts from those who have to pay the taxes. That budget contained some remissions, trifling in themselves but large in the aggregate to the less well to do, while the taxes on alcohol and tobacco were further increased. But in that budget there is a capital levy on incomes from investment. This is a political purchase tax, and it has established a precedent. The higher income groups will pay very heavily when this is added to the already heavy burdens they carry.
The socialists are blind to the damage being done their country. They think only of keeping power for their party and of putting good socialists into comfortable jobs. If these aspects were uppermost in the minds of the socialist government, however, it was otherwise with the general public. The orgy of extravagance, the lavish scale on which ministry officials live, says the National Review, the absence of thrift displayed by the government of Britain, all have appalled the electorate. They are asked to save. Why should they? What can be the use of saving when money is squandered in this way? Money and more money is to run out of the leaking government pool. It has to come out of the pockets of the people. That is what will be done here in Canada also, I am afraid. The government have taken- the sales tax off some articles of food1, which was a fine gesture, but they should have extended it to include clothing.
It is against this background that certain tax changes in the budget must be considered. We see these taxes in Britain, and over here we try to copy and imitate Britain in many ways. We see what happened at Geneva and all the rest of it. The present tax rate not only discourages saving; it incites people to spend whatever they have. With reference again to the special levy in Britain, this falls most heavily on the enterprising and the thrifty and at the- same time spares others, while the tax relief granted does the same thing.
I say here, Mr. Speaker, that I am for an empire policy. I agree with Mr. Casey, the outstanding Australian statesman. I am in favour of an empire conference on trade, defence and migration. As Mr. Casey said on April 18, we need a great empire leader who will go through the empire with a flaming sword. The United Kingdom is blind to the bright pictures and happy prospects tying

The Budget-Mr. Bentley
latent in the dominions, particularly in South Africa and Australia. It is vital that she should decentralize her population throughout the British commonwealth. Until she ceases regarding herself as an isolated community and plans her economy accordingly the people of the United Kingdom have little hope of rising above their present drab austerity. Mr. Casey went on, to say:
There are in England men of character, experience aiul vigour who are virtually unemployed. The empire's talent is at present wrapped in a napkin. British citizens could have the sun, moon and stars if they stirred out of their lethargy.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I can conclude in just a moment. Mr. Casey went on to say that they could again take their place in the country of nations as a great power b37 the policy he names, and I believe that is so. I suggest that Britain should help the dominions before giving help to any of these mandated countries, where her efforts have not been appreciated. As Lieutenant-General Sir Alan Cunningham said, but for outside interference Britain would have brought the Palestine problem to a happy ending, and so she would if she had been left alone to do so and not have been interfered with by the UNO, and the way Washington and the UNO changed so often about it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had quite an interesting debate on the budget. A week ago last evening the government rolled out their big gun and gave us quite a barrage. Then last Thursday the heavy artillery of the official opposition was brought up in the person of their financial critic. Since then we have had a series of smaller guns; then today the Liberals rolled out another big one and turned him loose on us.
I am not going to deal with many of the questions raised by those who have spoken previously, though after a while I am going to offer one particular criticism of the budget. Before doing so, I want to draw to the attention of the financial critic of the Progressive Conservative party some things he said to which I would not care to have to subscribe. Early in his remarks he dealt with the minister's predilection for the easy spending of the money under his control, and endeavoured to persuade the minister that he should reduce expenditures. He suggested that this could be done in several ways. I want to refer to two statements, the first

appearing on page 4240 of Hansard, where the hon. gentleman said in part:
I suggest to him, with every desire to be helpful, and I am sure he knows that that is always my wish, that there is only one way to economize, and that is to give people less money to spend.
I want to make it clear that at that time the hon. member was speaking of the money the minister made available to heads of departments. In justice to the hon. gentleman, I do not want it thought I am trying to show he was referring to the people of the country. Then, on the next page he went on to say:
. . . that is, he should not argue with people over what they would like to spend; he should tell the departments what he is going to allow them.
That may sound like a quite unimportant statement, but if that is the position the hon. gentleman would assume if he were Minister of Finance I should say that is as close to a financial dictatorship of this country and of a duly elected parliament as anything could be. The suggestion is that the Minister of Finance should tell the head of another department, for instance the Minister of National Health and Welfare:	"Here is the
money you can have. To the extent that you can replace with better clothes the rags of some unfortunate Canadian citizens with this money, you may do so; but beyond that you may not go." That is the implication of a statement of that kind.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? I am sure he does not want to be unfair.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does he not realize that I was suggesting purely a method? Of course I was not suggesting that the Minister of Finance would do it in any arbitrary or unthinking way, but that he would have his own means of arriving at what he thought was the proper amount. It was purely a matter of technique.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was not a question. However, the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has had an opportunity to clarify a statement that disturbed me a good deal. As I say, I should not like to see the Minister of Finance of this country have such powers.
Another thing the financial critic of the official opposition said was that the desire for security on the part of the Canadian people was stifling the spirit of adventure. He mentioned the fact that a poll taken among the people had indicated that about thirty-eight per cent of those questioned would like
The Budget-Mr. Bentley

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You do not object to that, do you?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

No. I am very glad that they have been helped to that extent; but I do say we should have that opportunity available to the fullest extent; so that all children who in primary and secondary schools have shown themselves capable and who wish to go ahead, should be able to do so, and should not be prevented because of failure of family finances to supply them with those things they require in order to continue their education.
The hon. member mentioned the matter of attempting to stir up class distinctions in this country, and thereby to bedevil the country. I can assure him that I agree in his dislike of those things. But again I wish to point out that we cannot expect Canadians, any more than other people, to be content forever with luxury on the hill, and mud shacks or slums, or whatever it may be, surrounding it. Wendell Willkie pointed that out in his book, and we can see it every day. My goodness, anyone who has worked among the people of this country must have seen the time when, through 5849-280
pure unfortunate circumstances, people have had to reduce themselves and their families to a meagre existence, not because of any fault they have committed in their work, or the industry in which they were engaged, but simply because of some circumstances over which they had absolutely no control. And when we pick intelligent and able people, and know they are willing to work, and when we suddenly find them reduced to a class of work which will not compensate them the way in which they should be compensated if they are to keep their families, we cannot blame them if at times they form themselves into classconscious groups and become extremely angry about conditions in the country which has reduced them to that position. As I say, I am not trying to be discourteous to the hon. member. I simply want to draw these things to his attention, because I know from the very decency there is in him he will see the justice of what I am saying.
I should like to make one reference to what was said by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), at page 4355 of Hansard. From his speech it was evident that the hon. member for Rosedale had only one criticism to direct against the government. His speech conveyed to me the idea that the government was not doing too badly in its general policies, but that if the hon. gentleman's party were in power they would do the same things but would do them much better. That was the impression I got from his speech. I will quote what he said on just one point, because I have not time to go through all his speech. He said:
I would point out, however, that the policy of double depreciation was another example of faulty planning.
This from a member who has never shown much inclination to favour planning of any kind! He goes on:
Hindsight shows it to have been totally unnecessary and to have aggravated the inflationary tendencies already existing in our economy. Had we needed to create employment, it would have been a fine thing, but once again our economic managers-	-
Meaning the government, I suppose.
-saw dimly through dark-coloured glasses.
I would point out to the hon. member for Rosedale that the government on the opposite side of the house has constantly taken from the big business interests of this country any guidance it has ever accepted from anybody. The chambers of commerce and boards of trade have more influence on the government of this country at the present time than have any other bodies.
The Budget-Mr. Bentley

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is rubbish, the same old story.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Results are what count. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. Every time this government passes legislation you can find commendation for that legislation in the pronouncements of chambers of commerce, or if you go back you can find recommendations from chambers of commerce and boards of trade for such legislation; but every time you find recommendations coming from agricultural groups or from labour unions you find the government fighting those recommendations to the last ditch.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: That is rubbish too, and nobody knows it better than my hon. friend.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall deal with that a little later when I speak of farm organizations. At the moment I wanted to point out to the hon. member for Rosedale that the people in whom he places his economic faith, the leaders of big business in this country, were pleased with the double depreciation feature and many other government policies when they came in; and if, as he says, hindsight is better than foresight, he and his friends in big business must be indulging in that hindsight, because now they are weeping at the results of some of the policies which they believed were good a few years ago.
I now come to the main part of my criticism of the minister's budget. I shall not bother referring to Hansard, because if you pick it up and read it through you will not find the matter to which I am about to refer mentioned in it in any way whatsoever. But before coming to the main part of my remarks, let me say that this budget gives no taxation relief to the lower income groups in Canada, and there is no assistance of any assured kind for the consumers of this country. True, the minister took off the sales tax, but without any assurance that the saving will be passed on to the consumer. The minister made that quite definite. There is no relief, not even a little bit of relief, for the kids of the country who, for their parties and so on, have to extract another two cents from the old man to buy a. soft drink. In fact there is no relief in this budget whatsoever for the vast majority of the Canadian people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
