speechtext: Drink milk.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We can moralize all we like, on what adults and kids should drink, but at their little social affairs the children like to imitate their elders by having something to drink. Their elders, of course, forbid them alcoholic drinks; so the children have the habit of using soft drinks, and the government comes along and takes $23,000,000, because people are trying to teach their children to be temperate. There are spiritual values in democracy, but every piece of legislation passed by this house is based on purely materialistic thinking, and it is time we put a little bit of spirituality into some of our legislation.
In the budget there is no suggestion whatsoever of any taxation relief for our co-operative organizations. There is no suggestion that the three per cent tax imposed on co-operatives two years ago is to be removed. Again I point out that that is one of the most unjust taxes that has ever been imposed on any body of people in this country. It is a tax which is entirely unjustified. I will grant that it does not put a heavy financial load on most of the co-operatives, although a few of them find it difficult to carry this tax load.
But it is not because of the financial load it imposes that I complain. The co-operative movement was absolutely built up as a free enterprise, non-profit business, and when that three per cent tax was imposed it put upon the statute book of this country a law which declares that co-operatives which claim to be non-profit, free enterprise organizations are profit-making institutions. I wish that this house and the government could see that point of view. Nobody invests in a co-operative organization for the sake of getting interest on the money invested. It is purely a case of a small or large group of people getting together and saying, we will build something of our own to serve us in some particular way, in order to save the money that we have in our pockets. But when they have saved their money this government comes along and says: Before you can get that money back into your pockets, a certain portion of it we are going to call profits, on which you must pay income tax. There is no justification for an income tax of that kind.
I have before me a number of resolutions, but I shall quote only one of them today, since the minister has given an undertaking that Bill No. 454 will come up shortly after the budget

The Budget-Mr. Bentley
resolutions are disposed of. Here is a resolution that was passed unanimously by the congress of the Co-operative Union of Canada, held in Saskatoon on March 9, 10 and 11, 1948. The congress of the Co-operative Union of Canada is a combination of the various co-operatives in this country and also includes the active and able council of co-operatives in the province of Quebec. In this resolution they ask that the recommendations the congress made on March 22, 1946, should be given effect to by legislation. They do not want the tax applied by the means I indicated a few moments ago. They do not want this applied to any co-operative which comes in this particular group which I am going to quote for the benefit of the house:
(1)	It is controlled exclusively on the basis that no member shall have more than one vote.
Mr. Speaker, there can be no more democratic organization in the world than a business organization in which every shareholder, regardless of the amount of his investment, has only one vote. No small group of individuals can control the policy of that institution. To that extent, that makes it a pure co-operative. I continue with the resolution:
(2)	The net surplus arising from member business after payment of expenses and setting aside of depreciation and necessary reserves is allocated among its members in proportion to the business by each with the association or organization, pursuant to a prospect held out in its act of incorporation, bylaws, or contract with its members. If an association or organization desires to place in reserve a sum in excess of that which the minister deems necessary the setting aside of such additional reserve shall not disqualify such association or organization from exemption from tax, but such reserves shall be subject to tax in its hands.
That is fair enough. They ask only for the necessary reserves; then, if they desire to get more, the minister shall decide in his discretion whether they need these extras, and even if he decides that they do, they are prepared to have these reserves taxed according to other corporation taxes. I continue:
(3)	The surplus so allocated is paid to the members in cash, or in such other form as the association or organization may by bylaw determine, provided that the amount so allocated be reported when required by the minister, and, if income of the member, shall be taxable in his hands in the year in which it is allocated.

In other words, if in the allocation of patron-
(5)	Not more than one-third of its business in any year is done with non-members.
A co-operative cannot very well refuse to deal with those who come into its place of business who may not be members; but if not more than one-third of its total patronage is from non-members, they believe they should qualify as co-operatives, as I have explained. If more than one-third is, it would be obvious that they could get to such a size in doing non-member business that they would be more in the nature of a profit-making concern than a co-operative.
(6)	Notwithstanding the foregoing, any association or organization shall pay income tax on that portion of its net surplus arising from nonmember business which it does not distribute to non-members.
That means that they are fair. They say that, even though we are a co-operative, and do not do business with over 33j per cent nonmembers; even if we do business with only one non-member we recognize that that business is profit business unless we return his dividends to him. If we do not return his dividends to him we recognize that the profit there is taxable in our 'hands, and therefore it is quite proper that it should be taxed. I continue:
The surplus of any association or organization directly or indirectly owned or controlled by one or more of the said associations or organizations shall not be liable to taxation under the said acts, provided it conducts its business or enterprise in the manner above set forth. Nor shall any patronage dividend distributed by it to its member associations or organizations be liable to be taxed in their hands if the member associations or organizations, in turn allocate the dividend so received to the members on a patronage basis.
That means, Mr. Speaker, if a number of co-operative associations federate themselves for the purpose, tve will say, of manufacturing some of the goods they propose to distribute through their local co-operative associations, then the earnings of the federated organization, if they are allocated back to the individual co-operative associations, and from there to the individual members, should not be taxable as income in the hands of either the federated co-operative or the individual co-operative which is affiliated with each, and shall become income only when it is private income in the hands of the individual who finally receives it.
That is my main criticism of the budget today, not because there is no other criticism,
The Budget-Mr. Wylie

but because other hon. members have dealt or will deal with the other features. I did not want this opportunity to pass without drawing to the minister's attention the need for abolishing the three per cent tax on cooperatives, which was imposed by his government in 1946.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I do not pretend to be a financial wizard; yet, after listening to the interesting and sometimes convincing speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) this afternoon, I am still convinced that the budget was what so many hon. members have said it was, a big disappointment, not only to the majority of hon. members, or perhaps I should say, to hon. members of the opposition, but to many of the Liberal members who, when the vote comes, will of course vote with the government.
It was a big disappointment to Canadians generally, the working classes and the farmers. We all realize how the cost of living has increased, and with no tax relief conditions will be much harder. While I must say that the farmers are perhaps better off at the present time than they have been for years, yet they have been more or less forced out of many lines of production because of the income tax. I refer particularly to hogs. The raising of hogs in the southern part of my province is almost out of the question. That has happened as a result of the income tax. That is one reason; another reason is the shortage of feed. In the raising of hogs on a farm, the feeding is done in the early hours of the morning and in the evening. Therefore it is really overtime work. The farmers complain that they are not going to raise hogs for Mr. Abbott. That is the general contention in my area.
The leader of this party, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), in his speech offered some good suggestions. I feel sure that if they were adopted they would ease conditions in this country not only for the working classes and the farmers but for everyone in general.
Here and there there was some trimming of indirect taxes, just enough to mollify the public and kid them into thinking they were getting something back from a generous government. This policy is always defended on the ground that it is anti-inflationary. It seems to me that the government does not want the people to keep the money they earn. The government says that the people will only spend it and send up the cost of everything, and thereby help to increase the market for scarce commodities.

The public could understand that reasoning in 1945, in 1946 and even in 1947. But this is 1948, three years after the war. Many goods are in fair supply now, but clerks are looking at each other and watching business walk by the window because the tax siphon is too efficient.
Goods are high priced, because wages and costs of materials are high and the sales and excise taxes are so heavy. The chances are it would take a fair-sized recession or depression to force them down to pre-war levels, and I am sure the government does not want either of those eventualities. The public possibly could take some more of this anti-inflation treatment if it were convinced that the government, while preaching, was doing a bit of practising, but the signs do not point that way.
Ottawa still keeps an army of temporary civil servants with no great display of economy. They are paid by taxes. Ottawa keeps expanding offices all over the country, competing for office space with business, and thus driving up rents. These inflated rents cannot help having some effect on increased prices. That is not the way to buck inflation, but it is the government way. The government does these things while it milks the average taxpayer. It says in effect, "You give your money to us. We do not want any inflation, no, sir, not in Canada, but it is O.K. if we do a little inflating of our own".
That is just about the way the public see it. The poor taxpayer would dearly love to have a little surplus of his own after listening to the surplus mentioned in this budget-$670 million. The taxpayer would even like to put a little bit away for old age. The conditions today for the average middle man are entirely different from what they were in the time of our fathers and our grandfathers.
I wonder if it occurs to the government that the average taxpayer today would like just that chance. It does not follow that if he got a cut in income tax and in other taxes he would buy all the scarce goods in sight. He might put away enough money so that he could retire and not be dependent on a $30 a month dole from the government, and I think that would be a good idea. The $30 might be eaten up as it is today when we are fighting inflation with the cost of living beyond the 150 index mark.
If the government must save us from ourselves, just as a means of siphoning money to prevent inflation, it should take the money not to spend it all itself but rather to give some of it back to the taxpayer. Compulsory savings were used in wartime for that purpose, and it could work today instead of having us robbed blind.

The Budget-Mr. Wylie
We have had comparisons of income tax with the United States, and according to the table that appears on page 4066 of Hansard there is little difference until you get over the $2,500 mark. That is as far as income tax is concerned. But it is the other taxes that we are concerned with.
We have the taxes on cars. We pay from $500 to $600 more for a Ford or a Chevrolet or a Plymouth and up to $800 or $900 on a Chrysler, above the price in the United States. That applies not only to cars but to many pieces of electrical equipment; one might say all of it. The same is true of farm machinery and many other items. When, therefore, we discuss taxation as between the two countries, I think the conditions are entirely different.
We must go farther than the actual income tax. Income tax today is, of course, doing nothing but taking the money out of our pockets so that we shall not have it to spend. That was done with the 25 per cent that was put on last fall on many goods; in fact, on almost anything you -wanted to buy. That was done for exactly the same purpose. It is true that the government has taken the admission tax of 20 per cent off theatres and the tax off some of these other things such as pari-mutuels, but most of the provinces have put it right back on. Alberta is the only province I know of that has not. Ontario is doing it; Saskatchewan has done it, and most of the other provinces are doing it. Alberta is not putting that tax on. I think that is to their credit. The minister expressed the hope that the provinces would not, but I believe legislation was passed by most of the provincial legislatures some time ago to get the tax when it was released by the dominion government.
The eight per cent sales tax could very well have been taken off completely. That should have been done two years ago. At the present time it is taken off certain items. I am sorry the minister did not see fit to take it off soft drinks, chocolate bars and candies, as the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) suggested. I think it is time the kiddies got back to their nickel drink. I have received many letters from manufacturers of soft drinks this year wanting this tax removed. I think the sooner that is done, the better.
There has been an announcement by the minister that interest will be paid on overpaid income tax. While the interest is very small, it may be some incentive, but I think the greatest incentive to make people pay the tax is the increase in the penalty. It is now up to seven and eight per cent.
The minister said, as reported at page 4067 of Hansard:
It is also proposed to increase the penalty rates applying to unpaid taxes from the present 4 per cent and 7 per cent to 6 per cent and 8 per cent respectively. These higher penalties will provide an additional spur to the payment of the proper amount of tax on the due date and contribute to greater equity as between individual taxpayers.
It may and it may not. I often wonder why the government does not pay something on the money it has deducted through the payroll system. It used that money in some cases for fifteen months with no interest paid on it, and that amounts to a substantial sum quite often. It also treats the wage earner or the man on salary in a way different from that in which almost any other taxpaying citizen is treated.
I think that when anyone hires out for $150 a month, he is entitled to that. That is an agreement reached between him and the employer. But along comes the government and says that so much income tax must be deducted at the source. It is about time that was discontinued, unless the government sees fit to pay about the amount of the penalties it imposes, either six or eight per cent. If that were done, it would certainly help. I hope the government will soon see its way clear to stop that tax deduction at source.
Getting back to the 25 per cent that was put on last November, I would point out that there is one thing that is doing; it is discouraging buying. It has stopped people from buying what they wanted and what they have done without during the war years. I refer particularly to frigidaires, gas refrigerators, cars, and many other things. A few minutes ago I mentioned the tax that has been put on cars. I have here the opinion of an authority, the president of the Ford Motor Company of Canada, Mr. Greig. This is what he has to say in connection with the 25 per cent tax:
The effect of "excessive" excise taxes on passenger automobiles eventually will be reflected in a dwindling market and must inevitably result in reduced employment in the Canadian motor car industry . . .
That is a statement by the president of the Ford Motor Company. Farther on he says:
This onerous excise tax was piled on top of the eight per cent sales tax, which remained unchanged . . . The government made it clear that the purpose of this heavy tax was to hold down-discourage, if you will-the buying of passenger cars in Canada and thus to conserve a proportion of the United States dollars expended for imported parts and materials used in their manufacture.
We strongly feel that effective import controls have removed the last vestige of need for an
The Budget-Mr. Wylie

excessive excise tax as a means of conserving United States dollars. The fact that our national surplus is in the neighbourhood of $800,000,000 is a clear indication the excise tax on automobiles is not needed for purposes of revenue.
That is from a man who, I think, really knows what he is talking about.
While I am on that subject of the shortage of United States dollars, there is one other thing I should like to mention. It is reported in the press, of course, by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that the ban on the export of cattle to the United States may be removed in the near future. That is one way of easing the dollar situation. The large ranchers in southern Alberta-with ranches that run up to 5,000 and 6,000 head of cattle- all agree that that should be done. They are quite willing to accept the Canadian price, but there is one thing they want and that is to be able to hold that market. That is our natural market. It is a market we have always depended on, especially in southern Alberta, because we are far removed from the heavily populated centres. By removing that ban, I am sure the government would receive much assistance. I think I would be quite safe in saying that $100 million or perhaps $150 million would be received, depending on the number of cattle allowed to go into the United States. That is our natural market in that area. Those ranchers are certainly hoping to see that release.
Coming back to the eight per cent sales tax, I am reminded of a statement that was made in this house back in 1931 when the Conservatives sat to the right of the Speaker and the Liberals to the left. This is what the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had to say in 1931 in connection with the sales tax which was put on at that time:
Where does my right hon. friend expect to get most of his taxation? He expects to get it out of the sales tax (4 per cent) and from the excise tax of one per cent on everything that comes into the country.
What does that mean? The sales tax, as we all know, bears most heavily on the great mass of the people, yet the wealthiest people are receiving a partial exemption on their income tax, and that additional burden is placed on the great body of the people through the sales tax . . . This is the deathknell of everything in the way of freedom of trade!

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And of the Liberal party.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wonder if the Prime Minister spoke to the Minister of Finance before this budget was presented. I wonder what he thinks of the eight per cent sales tax now in the light of the statement he made when he was in the opposition in this house back in 1931? Times

have a way of changing. I am quite sure that he feels that, now it is on, it might just as well stay there.
During this debate various subjects have been covered, and there is one that I want to mention in passing. It is our housing situation in this country. I want to make some criticism of the wartime houses that have been built in my city of Medicine Hat. We have seventy-five houses that are now just about completed and, Mr. Speaker, I would really call them shacks-but shacks that are costing, I imagine, between $5,000 and $6,000 each. There is no basement in them, as all hon. members know. Those houses are all rented to returned boys who went overseas and fought for us for five years. When they come back we offer them a house like that at a rental of $22.50 to $27.50 a month. I contend that those boys should have had something just a little bit better than that; and when they are paying their rental, I think it should be considered as another payment on a house they would eventually own. Some of those boys have come back without arms and without legs, moved into those houses and will be there for the rest of their lives paying rent.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Gibson) mention the trans-Canada highway. That is one way I can think of in which a part of that huge surplus could be used. It could be used in building a trans-Canada highway from one end of Canada to the other, that Canadians can use. On my trip home last year I covered part of it. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that between North Bay and Sault Ste. Marie it is a disgrace, and certainly is not doing our tourist trade any good. I have spoken to many Americans who have driven fifty or sixty miles on that highway, then turned around and gone back through the United States. That is poor advertising, and something it will take years to overcome.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni mentioned some very good points, and I hope the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Ho\ve), or whatever minister is responsible, will see fit to adopt some of those suggestions. On Monday morning of this week a motor cavalcade left Brandon on its way through to the coast. Those people stayed in Medicine Hat last evening and were to leave this morning. There were about seventy-five in the party when it reached Medicine Hat, where two more cars and ten other people were to join them. The party will continue on to Lethbridge, Nelson and right through to Vancouver, advocating the southern route for the trans-Canada highway. Those people realize that something must be done, and I think it is up

The Budget-Mr. Wylie
to the dominion government, which has ways of collecting money that the provinces do not have. I believe this should be made a national policy, as it is in the United States. If we leave it to the individual provinces one may build a hard-surfaced highway from end to end of the province, while another will not; that is the situation at the present time. So it is to be hoped that something will be done in that respect.
Before I conclude, I want to touch upon a matter I have discussed in this house every year since I have been here. That is the question of irrigation in western Canada. Irrigation is very important to the people of the drought area, and when we see nothing being done year after year we wonder just what the intention of the government is in that regard. We realize that a start has been made on the St. Mary-Milk river dam, and we appreciate what has been done. That dam will cost a million dollars or more, but many other things have to be done in connection with distributing the water to be held in that dam, and the sooner a start is made, the better it will be.
The local branch of the Canadian Legion took up this matter at the convention in Saskatoon this week. They think the attitude of the government with respect to irrigation in entirely wrong; that is, dealing with it more or less as a relief measure. Irrigation is much more important than that, and should not have to wait until we have unemployment in this country.
The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has told us about the sugar beets we could raise in that part of the country. If we had irrigation we could grow more sugar beets. Any vegetables that can be grown could be raised in southern Alberta, where we have ample sunshine. In addition, small fruits, all kinds of grains and grasses, hay and anything else you care to mention could be raised there, and I believe a greater effort should be made in this respect.
At the present time, of course, we have more or less to rely on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. That has been of great assistance and is certainly appreciated by many farmers in that area. But for what they receive through P.F.A.A. bonuses many of those farmers would be on relief. I was just looking at the report of the Department of Agriculture for the year ended March 31, 1947, and I noticed that, since 1939, under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act the farmers have been paid almost $73,000,000. Of course Saskatchewan received most of that money; but when we consider what is being expended
under that legislation, and when we consider what can be done by spending a few million dollars on irrigation, I believe the right policy would be to push ahead with irrigation just as quickly as possible.
Perhaps the government may want to use another method to make rain. Years ago we had a man named Hatfield in that area, and what he shot into the clouds to make it rain no one will ever know. A new method is being tested now, not only in this country but extensively in the United States; that is, the possibility of making it rain through the use of dry ice. I understand that the national research council is carrying on investigations along this line. Only the other day I had a resolution from the Medicine Hat chamber of commerce in connection with the use of dry ice for this purpose. This resolution was also sent to the government, and I hope they will study it very carefully. It is quite short, and I should like to read it:
Whereas it is now publicly known that the dominion government of Canada is favourably disposed towards carrying out investigatory experiments in Canada of dry dee bombardment of clouds to create artificial precipitation of rain;
And whereas the Medicine Hat chamber of commerce is firmly convinced that all that area adjacent to the Cypress hills in Alberta, which includes that of the city of Medicine Hat and district, is a district of heavy cloud formations during the greater part of the growing season;
And whereas we feel that this is the logical point to carry out investigatory experiments;
And whereas there appears to be the existing facilities for the said experiments, located in this area at the Department of Xational Defence experimental station, Suffield, Alberta.
Be it therefore resolved that we urge that these experiments be carried on within this area as early as possible.
We have all the facilities at Suffield, which is a national defence experimental station. We also have plenty of clouds in that area. Of course I realize that, to make these experiments a success, the clouds must be of a certain formation and at a certain height; but I hope those experiments will be carried on in this district this summer. I assure the house we would all be glad to see it rain in the first two weeks of July. That is the time we always need it, so I would suggest that the government carry out their experiments toward the end of June or early in July. If they can make it rain I am sure the people of that area will be thankful indeed.
In conclusion, let me say it is up to the government to improve conditions, and this can be done through our democratic system of government. I believe that is the only way to do it. We must make conditions in this coun-
The Budget-Mr. J. A. Ross

try such that we do not have to worry about communism or any other ism that might endanger us.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the annual 'budget presented on May 18 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is most disappointing to the average Canadian citizen. While the figures he set forth show a surplus of about $670 million for the past year, other adjustments bring that up to $727 million; and cash received from other sources added to the cash surplus brings the total up to $1,181 million, as mentioned by the minister.
With the high cost of living in Canada today, with the heavy taxation and with our dollar value at approximately sixty-five cents, these citizens of Canada are entitled to greater income tax exemptions than are now allowed in Canada. The federal tax in 1939 was $38.76 per capita, whereas today the federal per capita tax is $198. Last year the minister budgeted for a surplus of about $190 million, and the result at the end of the year was several times that figure. For the coming year the minister is budgeting for a surplus of approximately $489 million; I hope he is somewhat closer to the figure than he was a year ago.
In 1939, in round figures, there were approximately 46,000 civil servants with the government. Today there are over 150,000 persons in government employment in this country; and in that I include the civil service. We find a great deal of extravagance and wasteful expenditure of public money by the present federal government. The minister may say, "Where would anyone reduce those expenditures?" My colleague the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) spent a full forty minutes in discussing the national film board. I am not saying they do not render useful service, but I do say there is an extravagant waste of money in that set-up. The estimates this year show in this regard an expenditure of $3,537,000, or an increase of $776,518 over last year. I am sure that great savings could be made in this respect, and a useful service extended to the people throughout the country.
There has been sitting a special committee on prices, which committee many people across this nation believe is now a complete farce. Heavy expenditures are being made there to retain legal counsel, secretarial staff and help of other kinds. The committee has been sitting since February 10, and in those three and a half months has held about sixty sittings. The last statistical summary from the Bank of Canada sets forth the cost of living index, and it shows a steady increase
[Hr. Wylie.]
from month to month up to the present time. That increase is still climbing, just as if the committee had never sat.
On May 24, as reported at page 4324 of Hansard the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) placed a set of figures on record, and his speech was referred to this afternoon by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley). I shall have something to say about the minister's speech somewhat later in my remarks. The figures placed on record by the hon. member for Brandon show that, during the years 1939 to 1947 inclusive, sums paid to farmers of Canada in subsidies, bonuses, freight payments and other payments amounted to no less than $528,979. The hon. member gave the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) great credit for having brought about all this legislation.
I am not arguing about .the point the hon. member was attempting to make; but I take issue with the fact that he did not go farther and tell the plight of the farmers in his riding and throughout the Dominion of Canada because of the great loss they have suffered at the expense of legislation brought down by this government.
If we take all this into account, the difference during those years between what the farmer actually received for cereals, meats, dairy products and other products, and the average prevailing world market prices or United States prices is considerably over a billion dollars. In other words, the Canadian farmers have subsidized the consumers of Canada and of Great Britain with foodstuffs during those years to a value of over a billion dollars. That is a great contribution to be made by the agricultural producers of this country when one realizes that they were the only people so controlled during those years and the only producers in Canada today still kept in a strait-jacket by the government and forced to market under controls to certain designated countries, and that they are prohibited from shipping their produce to other countries because of embargoes imposed by this very government.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was discussing the amount which the agricultural producers of Canada had contributed since 1939 in subsidizing the consumers of this country and Great Britain. I want now to refer to the average losses suffered by the prairie farmers because of the United

The Budget-Mr. J. A. Ross
Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement from August 31, 1947, to April 31, 1948, which is in the present crop marketing year.
A comparison between the revenue received by the Canadian farmers, including producer certificate payments of twenty cents a bushel which are now being distributed, and the price of class 2 wheat averaged by months, shows a loss per bushel for the 1947 crop to date of $1.50 a bushel. There were 127.305,668 bushels delivered in those nine months under the agreement, showing a loss of $191,891,763 for the first nine months of this marketing year. On the same basis, wheat destined for domestic consumption within Canada averaged a loss of $1.50 a bushel. There were 54,755,418 bushels delivered, showing a loss to the producers of $82,401,104. Thus the prairie farmers in wheat alone, in the first nine months of the 1947-48 crop marketing year, subsidized the consumers of Canada and Great Britain to the amount of $274,292,867. That is quite a figure. Remember, this is the second year of the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement. The loss per bushel to the producers this year is almost double what it was in the first year of the wheat agreement. Those figures are on the record by the ministers of this government.
If the proposed international wheat agreement is carried into effect, it will be absolute proof that Canadian wheat producers will have no opportunity of regaining the hundreds of millions of dollars which they have already lost under present governmental marketing operations.
Producers within other exporting countries such as the United States, which will be a signatory to the international wheat agreement, received the benefit of prevailing world prices while they were at a reasonably high figure through these past years, and they took advantage of their situation. But the government of this country saw to it that our producers should not secure those prices. I have seen a copy of the agreement from Washington, and unless there are considerable changes made our producers will never regain any of this great loss which they have suffered. It is far too great a contribution to ask any one class of this nation to bear, much as we are agreed as to the necessity of keeping down the cost of living. Other methods could have been taken which would have assured that our agricultural producers would receive their fair share of the national income along with manufacturers and producers of other necessities of . life in this country.
This afternoon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley), who was minister of finance during the war years when much of this legislation controlling the farmers was brought into effect, spoke 5849-281
in favour of the present budget. He said that he thought this government should follow the example of the United States government and budget to pay off the national debt. If that be true, why not budget consistently for this purpose? Why was this suggestion not made a year ago when the minister brought down the budget? But there was no indication of any such thing at that time. Last year's proposed surplus would not indicate that the thought had occurred to any member or official of the government. When the present Minister of Justice was minister of finance no member of the government was more responsible than he for certain regulations which put the producers of this nation in a strait-jacket which prevented them from receiving world prices for their products. I admit that he received a lot of advice from his colleagues, but he was responsible for the legislation which came under his department. And now he suggests that we should copy the United States. I think he might well be a party to seeing that our farmers shall receive assistance on the same basis as United States producers are receiving assistance today and have received it through past years.
The Canadian government have refused and are refusing to allow the export of agricultural products from Canada to the United States, despite the fact that this trade would correct a great deal of our United States dollar exchange difficulties which the Minister of Justice mentioned this afternoon. He and his colleagues are more responsible for our exchange situation today than anyone else I know.
I shall certainly support the amendment moved by my colleague the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) that "this house is of the opinion that the government does not possess the confidence of the country." So much for the budget, because I do not want to repeat arguments that have been made by other members.
During the past week-end and early this week it was my privilege, along with other members of the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs, to visit the city of Saskatoon and attend the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion which is now in progress. Upon our arrival there last Saturday, we were informed of the passing of a great Canadian. May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to speak of him as one of ourselves, Comrade Colonel J. L. Ralston. He was a man of great courage, high principles and sterling character. To those who were not privileged to sit in this house with him, if they want real proof of his courage and self-sacrifice I suggest that they read the speech delivered by this great Canadian in the House of Commons on the evening
The Budget-Mr. J. A. Ross

of November 29, 1944, which will be found recorded in Hansard of that year at page 6657. He certainly proved what a great Canadian he was at that time by his selfsacrifice.
Following the drumhead service on Sunday afternoon, and at the ceremonial opening of the convention on Sunday evening, the legion hymn was sung, "Old Soldiers Never Die, They Simply Fade Away," and there seemed to be more significance than ever in that hymn on that rather sad occasion. I was happy to think that the first business transacted at the business session on Monday morning was the passing of a resolution of condolence to the widow and son in the sad loss of a great husband and father.
As I sat on Monday and listened to the legionnaires in that great convention of over one thousand delegates deliberating on their problems, problems created as a result of two great world wars, and thought of the present worldwide international unrest that was referred to by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he pointed out that we might, on short notice, have to expend a great deal of money for national defence in this country, although it was not evident, this was brought home to me, Mr. Speaker, and I decided that it was my duty to avail myself of the first opportunity in this chamber to speak of the international peace garden. I want to compliment the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews), because on July 11, 1947, he cited the history of this undertaking. He made his remarks during the course of the discussion of the estimates on parks and historical sites under the Department of Mines and Resources, and I wish to compliment him on his fine presentation at that time. I thought he did a much finer job at that time than he did last Tuesday afternoon in his budget address. Certainly he did much more for the interests of his constituents as a whole whom he has the honour to represent, and the citizens throughout this country.
I have never before spoken on this particular matter, but I wish to say that the area of the garden consists of some 2,340 acres, 1,452 acres in Canada donated by the Manitoba government and 888 acres on the United States side, donated partly by Washington and partly by the state of North Dakota. This garden is situated in the Turtle mountains, a range of hills rising to some 2,500 feet above sea level. They extend forty-five miles east and west and twenty miles north and south, and are located midway along that great undefended 3,987 miles of boundary line between Canada and the United States, and midway along the
[Mr. Ross (Souris).)
southern boundary of the Souris constituency which I have the honour to represent at present in this house.
The international peace garden is incorporated under the laws of Manitoba and North Dakota, and has been recognized by both Canadian and United States governments. Further work on this project should be the responsibility of the federal government; first, because the whole proposal is international. The dominion government has already expended, through the province of Manitoba, approximately $52,000 on this area. It is interesting to recall a paragraph of the speech from the throne at the opening of the Manitoba legislature on February 29, 1932, under the leadership of Mr. John Bracken who has always been an ardent supporter of this garden, and is now the leader of the official opposition of the House of Commons. He said:
A memorable event of the past year is the provision made for the peace garden in the Turtle mountain region of Manitoba and North Dakota. This international project ought to have a prominent place in the peace chronicles of the present era when every thinking person in the world is compelled to realize that one of the most important questions facing our civilization is that of world peace, friendship, and co-operation.
An editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune of that date said:
It is a worthy, a splendid project, and one that has the enthusiastic approval not only of the people of Manitoba and western Canada, but of other millions in both countries . . . Some of the most magnificent monuments in the world have been erected to commemorate lost causes, vanished glories and ruined hopes. A peace garden, let us hope, will symbolize in its own living beauty, ever more cordial relations between the two countries.
On July 24, 1932 the official opening of the garden took place and people were assembled from great distances in the central west, both Americans and Canadians.
I should like to give a few facts concerning the present status of this international peace garden. First of all, as to the board of directors for this year, 1948, I will just give the principal officers. They are as follows: Honorary president: W. V. Udall, Boissevain, Manitoba; president: D. G. McKenzie, Winnipeg, Manitoba; chairman: John A. Stormon, Rolla, North Dakota; first vice-president: M. S. Colquhoun, Deloraine, Manitoba; second vice-president: Russell Reid, Bismarck, North Dakota; treasurer: Lieutenant-Colonel A. J. Robbins, 496 Ash street, Winnipeg, Manitoba; assistant treasurer: John A. Stormon, Rolla, North Dakota; secretary: Myrtle Baldwin, Rolla, North Dakota; assistant

The Budget-Mr. J. A. Ross
secretary: E. T. Johnson, Boissevain, Manitoba; assistant secretary: Henry Sunderland, Dunseith, North Dakota. There are some seventeen directors from all parts of the United States and Canada scattered throughout these two great areas, which speaks well for the people in that area. The booklet goes on to point out that for 133 years this great stretch of boundary line between Canada and the United States has been a boundary of peace without warship, fort, soldier or gun. It states that:
Two great world wars, and the economic and financial problems arising therefrom, and possible military requirements in the future, are drawing these nations into continuous and closer collaboration and co-operation. This practical demonstration is proof positive that peace between nations is more than an idle dream; it is an accomplished fact.
Then it cites the various reasons why these sites were selected. One of the reasons was that of the natural scenic beauty of the area; second, the wide variety of trees, shrubs and wildflowers found growing there; third, the abundance of wild life, including birds, native to the district; fourth, the large number of small lakes located in the Turtle mountains; fifth, the location being almost the geographical centre of the North American continent; sixth, it being located on the only hard-surface highway running north and south across the continent, extending from northern Manitoba through the United States, down into Mexico, and extending into the countries of South America; seventh, no physical barrier, such as rivers, lakes, mountains or gorges, standing in the way of the free movement of people across the boundary in the area designated. Then it gives the pledge which appears on the plaque as follows:
To God in His Glory
We two nations dedicate this Garden and pledge ourselves that as long as men shall live, we will not take up arms against one another.
Then it says:
In addition to a beautiful garden, our plans contemplate the erection of an international peace tower as a symbol of peace between our two great nations, and a suitable war memorial to the thousands of young men and women who gave their lives in the last two world wars in the defence of everything we hold to be dear in life. Associated with this memorial is to be a little chapel where friends of loved ones may seek comfort and consolation.
Plans are being made for tourist accommodation, picnic grounds, public assemblies and recreational facilities.
Customs and immigration offices will be erected on the site to facilitate the movement of people across the boundary.
A great deal of public support is already manifest. Women's organizations, churches, service clubs, boards of trade, returned soldiers'
5849-281J
organizations and many similar bodies, as well as a large section of the public, are evidencing a desire to help in the promotion of this worthy project.
Large sums of money will be necessary. We are budgeting for $100,900 for 1948. Financial support must be forthcoming from governments, public bodies, business institutions and we hope from tens of thousands of peace-loving citizens.
There is much more in the booklet, but I do not want to take up the time of the house to read it.
More and more, may I say, will United States tourists be drawn northward by the magnetic attraction of our national parks. I noticed in the Christian Science Monitor of yesterday many pages devoted to the tourist trade, and the same newspaper on May 21 stated that in 1948 United States tourists are due to spend 115 billion. It sets out in a number of paragraphs the way in which this money will be spent, indicating that a good deal will be spent by tourists coming to Canada. The Canadian people are looking for a great part of that money which will be spent by tourists, and I do not know what could be finer than to have the bulk of these tourists come through that peace garden, with all that it signifies of sacrifice on the part of our peoples in the two world wars.
I wish to compliment the people who met from different parts of Canada and the United States and originated the idea, bringing about the organization and having it incorporated as they have done. May I emphasize the intriguing fact that, instead of being situated in the far east or in the distant west, this garden is located actually within thirty miles of the exact centre of the North American continent. Surely that is a fitting place for it, for this tall and commanding peace tower, proclaiming to the world the friendship between our two great nations.
Again I compliment the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) upon having dealt with the question so efficiently on the estimates last year. I could have waited and done so this year in connection with the estimates; but I thought it would be more effective, and I hope it will be, coming from him. I appeal to the minister to have this 8100,000 set aside annually for a period of years to create what the board has in mind, in the Department of Mines and Resources, under parks and historical sites. If that is done, I trust that the minister will give this matter the just consideration which it so well deserves. Surely it befits these two great nations and the peoples of these great lands; and therefore I make an earnest appeal, on behalf of the people of Canada, that we play our part, together with the people of the United States, in furthering this fine project.
The Budget-Mr. Burton

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and I no doubt can readily agree that the farmers of the country throughout the years have not received a fair share of the national income, yet I believe I would be correct in saying that the two of us have arrived at that conclusion by a different process of reasoning. And while I have no desire to delay the continuation of the budget debate by going into details with regard to what my colleagues and I in this group, on different occasions, have presented to the house as to the reasons why the farmers have not been receiving their fair share of the national income, and our opinion as to what should be done to rectify that situation, yet when the hon. member for Souris was speaking I could not help thinking of the time when the party to which he belongs was in office, and when I sold wheat at the lowest figure at which I have ever sold it in my life.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So they did all over the world.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will deal with that. I must say also that at that time I sold beef cattle, which were fit for the show ring, at such a ridiculously low price that it was a shame even to bother taking them to market. My hon. friend says that was the condition throughout the world. Yes, but we must remember that at that time there was a man high in the ranks of the hon. gentleman's party who promised the people of the country that he would blast his way into the markets of the world.
I cannot take time to discuss the many excellent speeches that have been made in this debate, but there is one to which I wish to refer, and that is the speech made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) this afternoon. He seemed to be somewhat concerned about something going on in this province and I wish to put him and his friends at ease. If I could follow the hon. member for Broadview he said this: "One matter to which I would call the attention of the house is the practice of non-residents coming into the province of Ontario and taking part in provincial elections". Later on he said: "In almost every newspaper I pick up there are reports indicating that some of my hon. friends to the left have been going around Ontario addressing meetings". While quite fairly enough the hon. member expressed the opinion that we had that right, yet he questioned the propriety of our doing so.
I wish to put the hon. member at his ease and say that, so far as my colleagues and I are concerned, we do not go to any meeting

in Ontario or in any other province of which we are not residents to address meetings unless we are specially invited by the people in those vicinities to go and speak to them. I also wish to assure him that on the odd occasion when I have accepted an invitation to address an Ontario audience I have made it quite plain that I had no intention of trying to tell them how to vote.
The hon. member should also remember that when people invite us to go and speak to them they have a right to know and to hear the story of Saskatchewan told by people who know the score; and if the hon. member for Broadview could assure us that certain people and certain interests in the province of Ontario would not go out of their way to distort the efforts our present government puts into solving our problems in the province of Saskatchewan, in all probability he would not be worried about so many of us taking part in speaking to the people.
Furthermore, may I say that if he could assure us that money from Ontario will not be used to try to influence the election in Saskatchewan during this coming month, then we could all feel a little more happy, especially if he could assure us that Trestrail and people of that ilk would not be using money that very often has been made off the industry of the people of Saskatchewan and of western Canada to tell us later on what is good for us, and in such a way that it is frequently obnoxious.
When the Minister of Finance, on the evening of May 18, delivered his budget address, I could not help feeling sorry that so promising a young Liberal minister should be placed in a position of such difficulty by having to present such a typical Tory budget. I must compliment the minister on having done a very good job on a very poor subject. I am quite satisfied that it was as distasteful to him as his budget is to the majority of the people of the country.
But my pity turned to amazement when a man who apparently adheres to the traditional Tory attitude, like the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). endeavoured to criticize the budget brought down by the present Minister of Finance. I could not help thinking that if the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and his colleagues were on the other side of the house, in all probability, with the possible exception of a few minor details, they would have brought down a similar budget. We can be quite certain of the fact that it would not have been any better; in all probability it would have been

The Budget-Mr. Burton
a still more bitter pill for the common people of this country.
As time goes on, a person cannot help noticing that those people who prefix "progressive" to their party label are coming closer and closer to the Tories that are only Liberal in name; in fact, in some provinces of this country they are already in the same camp.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What do you mean?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In my own province of Saskatchewan these people are in some places arranging saw-offs among themselves in an attempt to delay the march of progress.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do they call themselves "Independents"?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what they do in Alberta.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They call themselves fusion candidates.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Confusion candidates.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In some places they do not even go to that extent. One might say they are running on the same ticket. In dual member constituencies they have arrangements whereby one candidate will be a Liberal and the other one a Conservative.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you cannot tell them apart.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is just what I was trying to tell the hon. members; more and more is it becoming evident that one has greater difficulty in telling them apart.
When my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) moved the subamendment for our group and later on was followed by other colleagues from this group, not only did he and they place on the record our want of confidence in the government; the amendment also stated the reasons why and wherefor we considered that the government was doing a poor job. I will not endeavour to retrace all the arguments that have been brought out. I will not endeavour to search out any other defects in the budget. But as all hon. members will know, our case has been made clear and plain, and we have no hesitation in submitting the stand that we have taken to the people of this country.
May I refresh the memory of hon. members. When my leader moved his amendment, it was as follows:
That the said amendment be amended by inserting after the word "government" and before the word "does" in the second line of the amendment, the following words:
. . has failed to relieve the excessive burden of taxation on the low-income groups of the Canadian people:
(a)	By failing to increase the amounts of exemption from income tax from the present levels to $1,250 for single and $2,500 for married persons, and
(b)	By failing to remove or substantially reduce the burden of sales and excise taxes which bear most heavily on those suffering from low income and the present high cost of living.
And further, the government has failed to establish a public investment board to assure the channelling of capital investment into socially desirable projects as a means of maintaining full employment, increasing production and raising the standard of living of the Canadian people, 'and . . ."
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that any progressive-minded member who is desirous of voicing the opinion of the people he has the honour to represent will certainly be obliged in his own mind to support that amendment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what you think.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While I could go on and aggravate the Minister of Finance by picking here and picking there at this umbrella budget, as some call it, and point out many other parts that are obnoxious to the people of Canada-in fact, I would say a great many features of the budget were not necessary- yet, what is the use? If by this time we have not convinced enough members on the other side of the house that the people of this country do not approve this budget, then, so far as I am concerned, I am prepared to take the vote and abide by what, the majority decides. But let me say this much to hon. members through you, Mr. Speaker:	the
people of Canada are not satisfied and they will make good use of the opportunities that are presented to them to register their protests.
Before I resume my seat, there are one or two matters that I should like to deal with which are only indirectly connected with the budget. The first, I may say, was referred to by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) the other day when he was taking part in this debate; and today I believe it was again referred by some other hon. members, including the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie). The hon. member for Comox-Alberni, as reported at page 4310 of Hansard of May 24, suggested this:
1. Set up a federal highway commission which would designate the highways to be considered as links in the trans-Canada highway system.
Later on he said this:
Mr. Speaker, the creation of such a federal or trans-Canada highway board is a step which I am sure would meet with the approval of every member of this house, as may be confirmed by reference to speeches made by members on ail sides during the past years. The arguments are too numerous and too well known for me to repeat them at this time, but I know that every Canadian looks forward to the day when
The Budget-Mr. Burton

there will be a highway across Canada, from sea to se!a, from Yarmouth in Nova Scotia to Tofino on the west coast of Vancouver island.
I fully concur in that. I would go even further and say this. Our dominion government has let Canada lag at least fifteen to twenty years behind the times in not having provided for such a federal board of highway commissioners. That board, as the hon. member suggests, would endeavour to settle little, petty, local arguments as to whether this highway should run here or there. I would go even further and say that the federal government, even in this budget, should have made provision so that that board could have had the wherewithal to operate and be of assistance to the provinces in having a trans-Canada highway system constructed.
It is all very well for the minister to say, as he did in his budget speech, that this is not a time to branch out into some of these activities. I agree with him in part in that respect. But let me draw to his attention the fact that we have found it to be the case, not only in our farming activities but in our other business activities, that if you do not make use of good times in order to make your plans to revamp and repair your machinery, then, when the rainy day hits you, you will find yourself in a difficult position. That is why during the period often referred to as the hungry thirties, when we had men practically wasting away in relief camps, no such works were undertaken; nothing was ready so that they could start doing useful work. The excuse was that there was no money, whereas we should have had the machinery ready and should have had arrangements made for the materials and the necessary finances. If that had been done we would not. be lagging behind our friends across the border by at least fifteen or twenty years.
As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni says, every Canadian is looking forward to the day when we shall have a trans-Canada highway from sea to sea. In my opinion a board of federal highway commissioners would, in the first place, work with the provincial governments to co-ordinate their activities in that respect, and could arrange material and financial assistance for them as well. They could also decide, for example, whether from Winnipeg on east, through that long stretch of unproductive country, it would be desirable to have a four-lane highway connecting with the central and eastern parts of our country, or whether it would be more desirable to have the highway branch out to cover different parts of that territory. If you look at a map you see that in all probability such a highway system would have to go through Winnipeg, which for more reasons than one is referred

to as the gateway to the west. Practically, speaking, there is no cither way to get to the west except through Winnipeg or by coming close to it. A little further west, however, you can branch ou't, and as you go further west you can go more to the north and still be in settled, productive territory. Here again I contend that we should not be satisfied with just a little ribbon of highway across the plains, which we may call a trans-Canada highway. We should have a system of highways adequate to take care of that great western plains country; and since highway construction in that area would be easy and comparatively cheap, there is no reason why we should not have both a southern route and a northern route.
However, Mr. Speaker, you cannot expect the provinces to do this. It is really a federal job. My own province of Saskatchewan has about thirty-eight per cent of the total surveyed roads of Canada, but at the same time we have only about seven per cent of the total population. How can we be expected to give proper road facilities and services to our own people and, in addition, do the job the federal government should do in providing a trans-Canada highway? So I repeat that even in this budget provision should have been made for such assistance to the provinces. We are endeavouring to do what is possible, but there is a limit to what the provincial governments can do. During the past four years new work undertaken and reconstruction work on highways in our province amounted to 1,680 miles, and this year a tremendous building program is contemplated. During the past four years we have regravelled approximately 4,000 miles of highways, and during the past three years we have tripled the total mileage of hard-surfaced roads in the province. Quite frankly, the total mileage of hard-surfaced roads was very much limited until a few years ago, but at least we have made a start in that connection.
' The other question with which I should like to deal is also of vital interest to the people not only of my constituency but of practically all of western Canada; that is, the Hudson bay route. In the first week of August of last year the Hudson bay route association, in co-operation with the government of Saskatchewan and with the magnificent assistance of the Canadian National Railways, put on an excursion to Churchill. I had been wanting to go to Churchill ever since the road was opened, but something always interfered with my plans. I am happy to say, however, that last August I had an opportunity of making that trip; and I was so delighted with what I saw that if another excursion is held this year I want to

The Budget-Mr. Burton
make the trip again. At this time I should like to extend a hearty invitation to hon. members from Ontario and Quebec and the maritimes, who may have time to spare, to join us on that trip. If they do they will see for themselves that there we have not the white elephant a great many people would like to make it out to be. I can show them that, with the possibilities which now exist, if only we get a fair deal, the road, the port and the route will be an asset not only to the western provinces but to all Canada.
When the excursion train left Regina last August three ministers of the provincial government were on board, and I am happy to say there was also a member of the Alberta government, who, I believe, since has been called to his reward. In that connection I should like to make a suggestion to my hon. friends from Alberta. I noticed that Hon. Mr. Fallow had with him a very nice little movie camera, and I am sure he obtained many fine pictures. Possibly my hon. friends could intercede with the members of his family and make arrangements so that the Hudson bay route association might be able to use the films he took at that time.
Proceeding in a northerly direction the Hudson bay special stopped at Saskatoon, where many others joined the party. From there we went on to Prince Albert, where the citizens and the board of trade gave us a hearty welcome. They realize that even at Prince Albert we are not yet half way up the province. They know the tremendous possibilities for the development of that northern country.
From Prince Albert we went to The Pas, Manitoba, and again we were well received. From The Pas we had a side trip arranged for us which took us to the mining town of Flin Flon, on the border between Manitoba and Saskatchewan. I might add that we were keenly interested in this, and spent several hours in this mining and smelting town. I can assure hon. members that many of our prairie dwellers had a little better idea of the tremendous wealth in that northern section of western Canada.
May I add that in the sight-seeing trip I had the good fortune to be in a motorcar driven by one of the officials of the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company. Answering our questions he told us that, in so far as their experts and surveyors were able to ascertain, not only his children but his grandchildren would have no need to worry about the mineral ore being played out or depleted in their lifetime.
From 1940 to 1945, the war years, when we needed so much the production from our mines, this area milled 12,262,838 tons of ore.
That produced 475,125,604 pounds of copper and 605,116,521 pounds of zinc, as well as some other valuable metals.
We had to return to The Pas to take the Hudson bay route which starts at The Pas and runs in a northeasterly direction. For the information of hon. members, let me say once we were on what is properly known as the Hudson Bay railway, in spite of our having only a freight locomotive of ordinary size drawing our large excursion train, the ride was most comfortable and agreeable. In fact neither the Canadian National nor the Canadian Pacific through northern Ontario is anywhere nearly as comfortable from a riding standpoint as is that stretch of road from The Pas to Churchill.
Between The Pas and Wabowden, the first divisional point outside The Pas, is an area in the neighbourhood of 5,000,000 or 6,000,000 acres of arable land awaiting settlement. In addition to that, there is a tremendous amount of forest products and products from lakes and streams, besides undiscovered and, in some places discovered but undeveloped, mineral resources.
Mr. MaciNICOL: And a fine stand of timber.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, the hon. member is quite correct; there is a fine stand of timber.
I contend that the Hudson Bay railway has the potentialities of making that port a paying proposition, just because of the natural assets in that part of the country.
Furthermore, when we got to Gillam, the next divisional point-and remember, this was in the first week of August-only 150 miles from Churchill, our train stopped for a short time for servicing, during which time the passengers on the excursion train got out to walk along the right of way, and they were picking ripe strawberries. That, in the first week of August!

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No cream?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They were so delicious we could do very nicely without cream or sugar.
We proceeded north from Gillam. In that area are millions of horsepower going to waste because of a lack of development of the waterfalls and rapids which could easily be developed. When we arrived at Churchill almost all of us began to see the sights, which we covered as much as we could from that time until the following evening. Included in our sightseeing was the elevator. Incidentally, let me add that I was informed by some of the superintendents that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was responsible for some of the up-to-date equipment
The Budget-Mr. Burton

installed in that elevator. I was told that at one time, and in the space of four minutes, they can unload four carloads of grain.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister was active in private enterprise when he put that in.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would say that whatever the minister did because of his inventive genius and engineering ability is now given a chance to work for the people as a whole. He does not, like some other hon. members, always follow the line of private enterprise.
We have there an institution which is not a private enterprise, but it is a credit to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to anyone else who had anything to do with the erecting of the elevator and the building of the railway.
We were invited to visit the airport and army base being operated at that place. Let me say to hon. members who are sometimes worried about our Yankee friends having a few people up at that base that in my view they are unduly alarmed. From what we had an opportunity to see, the men stationed there were being well cared for and were doing a job which must be done if we are to develop that northern country as it should be developed. While it is true that friendly relations might at times become too friendly, at the same time I would repeat that I do not think in this instance we have anything to worry about.
I took a number of snapshots along the line and at Churchill. We have not time to go into all these details, but I might add that, while there, we saw many of the so-called white whales. I mention this now because some time ago a good many people were excited about whale oil. Right there at our back door we have whale oil available, if we only make arrangements to secure it.
The trip back was arranged so that the train covered in daytime almost the same mileage we had covered at night when going up. The result was that we saw about all the territory and the surrounding country so far as it was humanly possible to do on such an excursion.
There was one thing that struck me forcibly on that trip. In the first place, there were very few young people on board. Most of us were either middle-aged or going on to advanced years. But everyone seemed to be determined to see as much as possible in the short time available. With very few exceptions, they were pioneers of the west, and the impression they gave me was that they had at last the opportunity to fulfil the dream of a lifetime by making a trip to their own port of Churchill on Hudson bay. For some of us it was the first opportunity we had of having our feet on

the deck of a boat travelling in deep water, and it reminded me that those of us who travelled in prairie schooners in days gone by never got seasick.
The possibilities of trade between the prairie provinces and the maritimes are immense, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, that we shall continue to develop this route. I am satisfied that if it is given an opportunity to show what it can do, it will be an asset not only to the people of western Canada but to the country as a whole.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the interesting things about the budget debate is the notable travelogues to which we are treated, which give us a better appreciation of the great possibilities of Canada. But I could not understand just why the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) referred to this budget as being an umbrella budget. I did hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in presenting the budget, speak of laying something away for a rainy day. But my conception of an umbrella is something that gives you protection from what otherwise might be described as a thorough soaking, and I certainly do not feel that this budget measured up in any respect to that description. It might just as well be a totem pole as an umbrella for any protection it affords to the taxpayers of Canada generally.
I wish to comment briefly on the reference of the hon. member for Humboldt to a national highway. With all due deference to the present plans for beautifying Canada's capital, which, after all, is entitled to consideration because we are a proud people and want to make our capital as attractive as possible within due bounds, I can think of no more fitting memorial to the gallant sons and daughters of Canada than the building of a national highway acroas this country. As we are becoming more conscious of ourselves as a nation, surely we owe it to ourselves to guarantee that we can travel in our own country from coast to coast, without detours into another country and being compelled to declare what we are taking in and bringing out. At the present time many such detours are necessary.
The hon. member also referred to the vast areas beckoning the settler. As I listened to him I could not help wondering how the C.C.F. party would attempt to justify their bitter opposition to immigration, until we had housing and other comforts of life available for our new settlers. If we had attempted to build our future on that theory, Canada would never have been. O.ur forefathers came to this country with no homes to go to or anything else, but they were prepared to address themselves

The Budget-Mr. Case
to the task of hewing homes for themselves out of the forest and suffering hardships and privation in laying the foundations upon which future generations have continued to build up this country. Theirs was not an easy task in any sense of the word.
I often think of that when I hear my C.C.F. friends criticizing the Premier of Ontario for his plan to bring into this province 7,000 immigrants a year, but apparently Ontario must now take a back seat to Alberta which has indicated a desire to secure 400,000 immigrants from the British isles in the next ten years. I agree with the. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that every effort must be made to bring these people to where the food is to be consumed rather than to assume that we can constantly be shipping the food to them in other countries.
I think I should say, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance has proved himself to be at least courageous, because a few nights ago he presented to the house and the people of Canada a budget which certainly is not popular in any part of Canada that I have had the opportunity to visit. Nor can I think it is very acceptable to the Liberal party, regardless of the fine effort made this afternoon by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), a former minister of finance, in seeking to defend the position taken by the present Minister of Finance.
But to prove, Mr. Speaker, that this government have no sound formula of budgeting for expenditures and receipts, in the three years I have been here they have always been hundreds of millions of dollars out in their anticipated receipts. The last budget brought down by the Minister of Finance was only about S700 million out. Two years ago, when the present Minister of Justice was minister of finance he was prepared to budget for a deficit. How times have changed! Now the Minister of Justice, when we are seeking to bail ourselves out of a difficult situation, recommends and endorses the present proposals of the Minister of Finance to budget for a substantial surplus. Just how much they know about what they are doing is hard to understand. For instance, I was amazed to hear the Minister of Justice say this afternoon that, by raising the succession duties exemption from $5,000 to $50,000, he had been astounded to discover that it would mean a loss of only $5,000,000 in revenue. After years and years in the portfolio of minister of finance, he was amazed to make that discovery! But a mere $5,000,000 meant something to people some time ago.
I can think back to 1932 in the province of Saskatchewan when the then provincial
treasurer, Mr. Murdock MacPherson, carried on the affairs of that province with $12,000,000; and while Saskatchewan has many advantages today by way of social services, and such things as they are now seeking to tell the electors about, nevertheless last year it raised and spent more than $57,000,000. That is quite a far cry from $12,000,000. I suppose, so long as the people are getting some benefit from it, we must accept it.
However I am one of those who is not in any sense disappointed with the budget. I heard the stories on the street that there was likely to be a surplus of $750 million, and so on. I knew then that we were standing on rather thin ice. I knew that if the Minister of Finance was consistent, he could not lower taxation.
