I doubted whether he would be consistent, because there has been a lot of turning about on rather short notice in this House of Commons, but when he indicated to the House of Commons that his purpose in putting on the 25 per cent excise tax was to drain off purchasing power I knew that he could not be consistent and return anything to the people of Canada in the wTay of lessening taxation; otherwise he would be defeating the tax he had imposed by radio on November 17 last. Therefore I think we have just about what we might have expected.
I want to make this observation. I think it is a sad commentary, and it must mean a great deal to the Canadian people to know that we now have arrived at the place where, by interference and regulation, the government imply that they are no longer prepared to trust the Canadian people; that they must regulate their very lives; that they must draw off their purchasing power; in other words, that they must stem the trend toward inflation in this country. It seems to me so foolish to take the stand that we can regulate or beat inflation by draining off purchasing power. If the government had been anxious to serve a useful purpose, to play fair with the Canadian people, they would have reinstated, or so far as I am concerned they should never have abolished it, compulsory savings, if that was necessary, because then there would have been something laid by for a rainy day.
I am one of those who have come through the ranks of municipal government. We discovered long ago that if a municipality were allowed to budget for substantial surpluses the natural tendency would be to find some place to spend that money. That is the general trend when you allow governments to build up huge surpluses; and with an election in the offing next year, or possibly before that- although I doubt whether they would dare face the Canadian people on a budget such as that
The Budget-Mr. Case

brought down in this house recently-it could be possible that a great many favours might be provided by the huge surplus indicated.
Of course, if the Minister of Justice was correct in suggesting that this surplus might be continued for a number of years, I suppose from a purely economic point of view, there might be some justification for the attitude he was taking. I have at least been consistent in this regard. Even last year I urged the government to give evidence of faith in our country by budgeting for a deficit, because I felt that it would indicate to all and sundry that we had faith in our people and in our productive capacity. The productive capacity of Canada is positively immense; but as long as we hamstring the people with intolerable taxation we shall have this degree of labour unrest, we shall have this sense of confusion and lack of direction which is evident at the present time on all sides by our businessmen, and we are more apt to have a higher degree of inflation than we would have if we were to build up our productive capacity. In other words, up to the present time the people have been living in expectation of something they have not received.
One can understand that with the cost of living increasing, with taxation at an all-time high, with a huge surplus, which the government boast is the greatest on record, and yet no evidence of tax relief, it has a deadening and sickening effect on the whole Canadian economy; because, after all is said and done, it is all right to boast of surpluses; it is all right for the Minister of Justice to be critical, but by the very motion that has been made by the financial critic of this party we say that we have no confidence in this administration, and therefore we certainly have no confidence and trust that the surplus the government are seeking to fake from the Canadian people without any sense of direction will be spent wisely. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, nothing would have done more to stimulate production at the present time than to have cut straight across our taxation barriers and to have taken this country out of its present dilemma.
All through the budget address, and again this afternoon in the speech of the Minister of Justice, I heard many references to the United States of America. I have nothing but the greatest admiration for our great neighbour to the south, but I do not think our Canadian people should be poured into a mould and held in a strait-jacket just to satisfy some foolish whim we might have with respect to the United States economy.

For instance, this afternoon the Minister of Justice said, in effect-and I am not going to quote him exactly-if we had kept our dollar at par that we would be going into debt to a foreign country. Let us see how well the present administration have succeeded in that regard. I want to remind you, Mr. Speaker, and this House of Commons, it was not very long ago that, for the first time in history, Canada borrowed $300 million from a foreign power. This is the firkt time we have ever been in debt to a foreign government. If the government feel that their present policy is succeeding, I for one fail to recognize it.
The minister spoke of United States citizens who bought our bonds as a good investment. Certainly they bought those bonds with a $1.10 dollar. They bought those bonds on speculation that the Canadian dollar would return to par, and they sold those bonds back on the Canadian market in such numbers when the dollar was at par that the Bank of Canada was forced to lower the bids on Canadian bonds. That was what the Canadian investor had to pay for our regard for the United States economy.
What we want, Mr. Speaker, is an honest dollar. That is my plea tonight. The moment you build an artificial structure under your money you are affecting the whole basis of your economy. I think I have had sufficient experience to be able to labour that point if I cared to do so, because it is not a question of where you are going to nail this dollar. We had a tremendous trading advantage, a trading advantage in the markets of the world. So long as the United States dollar was accepted as the standard of value, all the markets of the world lay open to us. It is all right to say that we would have bought less from Great Britain or that the British exporter would not have had the same access to our markets. I fail to see that, if the United States dollar remained at the standard value of $1.10.
In other words, the greatest advantage any nation possesses is the right to regulate its currency in relation to its trading advantages in the world's markets. I suppose that is one reason why the top-heavy influence at Bretton Woods and the international bank determined that no country could depreciate its currency by more than ten per cent without the consent of the bank; but Canada was in a very strategic position. We had a ninety cent dollar to go into the bank with, which by the same token would provide us with the right of devaluing that dollar still further. In other words, we could not have an eighty-one cent dollar.

The Budget-Mr. Case
It does not have the same effect on the home market. Just imagine what the Minister of Justice said this afternoon-that they levelled the Canadian dollar because of the tendency toward inflation in the United States. He said that our Canadian importers were buying larger quantities in that market because they feared inflation, and right on the very eve of the time they feared inflation most he said to Canadian importers, "Here is another ten cents on your dollar; go and buy more and more." So why would they not drain off more United States dollars? The government bonused the purchase of goods in the United States by adding that ten cents on. The proof of the pudding is in the eating, and we have discovered that by our interference with the true level of our dollar, by our interference with the desire to have an honest dollar, we have interfered with our whole internal economy. There was no cry from the gold mines or the basic producers before we levelled the dollar. Now that we have levelled the dollar, we have to have a group of bureaucrats going up and down the country checking the books of the gold producers to find out how much gold they have produced in a certain basic period in order that they may be entitled to the bonus which the government says is in store for them.
Last but by no means least-I tried to copy this as carefully as I can, and I believe I have it verbatim-the Minister of Justice said: "But it would be undesirable, I feel sure, having in mind public opinion in the United States, to have a situation arise such as this: that the people in the United States should be keeping their taxes up to the high levels they have now attained, and that Canada, not contributing toward European recovery by way of credits, should seize the opportunity to push her taxes down and cash in on the situation in such a way that we would inevitably be severely criticized and penalized by others."
I do not think there ever was a time in history when the United States had to lean upon the philanthropic attitude of the Dominion of Canada. Generally speaking, they have been able Jo forge ahead for themselves-as a matter of fact, a little too much so-and it is a sad' commentary that our government was so much concerned about the economy of the United States, who today are looking for markets for their goods and trying to have someone drain off their -dollars in order that they might return as purchasing power. It is, I say, a sad commentary that we should be so much concerned that we would feel that we were [DOT]taking advantage of them by pushing our
taxes down. It is a most unfortunate fact, but all Canada is to be penalized because the United States dollar or the United States tax rate is not lower.
The minister forgets, although he made some comparisons, that income taxes are much lower federally in the United States than in Canada. He was inclined to confuse the issue by introducing a note with respect to state taxes. There are other things he overlooks: for instance, the fact that a motorcar of the same manufacture costs from $600 to $900 less in the United States than it does in Canada. We are paying a very fine price for our tie-in with the United States economy.
I certainly wish to do everything in a co-operative sense so that we may carry on together; nevertheless this country offers a great challenge to everyone, and when the minister seeks to fix our Canadian dollar at par with the United States, I resent very much his interference with the natural flow of trade and the placing of a 25 per cent embargo or restriction or excise tax on the Canadian dollar in the home market because, he says in effect, our dollar is worth 100 cents in the United States market. After all, this is a mere joke because our Canadian dollar is discounted at as high as fifteen per cent in a neighbouring city like Buffalo. He says that our Canadian dollar will be held at par in the United States markets, but by the same token he says it is worth only seventy-five cents in the home market in Canada.
I say to the government:	If that is your
idea of providing an incentive for Canadian producers; if that is your idea of providing more take-home pay for the worker in industry; if that is your idea of giving our farmers a break, then it will be written in history that it is the best formula you had to offer. But I think our people are entitled to a better break than that, particularly our farmers; and I plead on their behalf, because I like to feel that I am their spokesman in this House of Commons in so far as I represent them in my riding. I plead that they be given a larger exemption in respect of income tax than is generally provided for other citizens.
You may say that this is difficult to work out, but the Minister of Justice put ideas into my head. He said that huge surpluses did not go to cabinet ministers. I never thought they did, but he suggested it. Well, they have provided $500 more in the way of exemption for those of sixty-five years of age and over, and it does seem to me that a larger exemption for farmers can be justified,
The Budget-Mr. Case

because the farmer and his family all contribute to the welfare of their enterprise, no matter how small the individual share may be. I can remember as a boy seven years of age working on the farm, when I first learned to milk and to help to look after dairy cows. No matter how small the individual's share may be, they all play their part; and I think the government would be making a fine contribution, something that would be greatly appreciated by our farmers, if they fixed the exemption for farmers at a higher level than that accorded other classes, having regard to this one example I have given, where all the members of the family contribute to the family income.
Another thing I should like to see dealt with is this. I would make sure that this disability with respect to married women was removed. Only this government could think of a scheme like that, whereby they treat married women in a different class from other citizens. They say in effect, "You as a married man will have an exemption of $1,500. but if your wife has an income of over $250 you will deduct from your normal exemption the excess she has over $250."
That, too, has a restraining effect on the contribution married women could make, particularly in hospitals and in other fields of endeavour, and it is unfair. I do not think any married man would object to paying his tax on the basis of a single man if his wife had a taxable income, and no one other than this government could think of a deal of that kind whereby they charge a man a luxury tax for having a wife who has an income.
Another thing I am greatly concerned about is this. There is in effect, on the statutes of the country, a law which provides that every person must accept the family allowance. In making that statement some time ago, the Minister of Justice, then minister of finance, said it was not compulsory. It is not compulsory, but if you do not take it they will say you have taken it anyway. How will you get out from under? I do not think it is fair, and I suggest that there should be a certain level, say $3,000 or something like that, beyond which one would not be required to accept the family allowance unless he cared to do so.
The family allowance is something I have been inclined to criticize, not so much the benefits provided as the administration of it. I still feel that it was wrong in the first instance. I feel that the dominion government should have passed enabling legislation, so that any provinces which wanted to take advantage of the family allowances could have passed the necessary legislation to bring themselves within its influence. The administration then would

have been provided through the present social service set-ups within the provincial governments, through that of the old age pension and the mothers allowance. But no. We have now a unitary system and it is bad for this country. Dual administration would have been much better; because I am not too sure but that the time may come when those who are probably a little more radical than even the Liberal's may bid for votes on an increase in family allowances, and hon. members can see just how dangerous it may be. So I feel that there is room for adjustment there. I would certainly plead with the government to give consideration to that particular phase of our economy.
In closing, may I say I feel that the government should give immediate consideration to the references made by the hon. member for Humboldt to our vast resources. Certainly we have there an opportunity to provide something by way of leadership for our people, to encourage them to roll back our great frontiers and to benefit by the rich resources of the nation. Those resources can be turned to good account by providing our people with the services and other securities they are looking for.
Recently some of us, while guests of the board of trade of the city of Toronto, were privileged to visit Sunnybrook military hospital. That is a remarkable institution. There are miles of corridors. It covers acres of ground, and I understand that it will cost, when completed, between $7,500,000 and $9,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Between $7,500,000 and $9,000,000, I understand. But it will provide a haven for over 900 veterans. It is a marvellous institution and certainly is a tribute to those who conceived the idea of it and those who brought it into being. It was one of the highlights of our trip. When I think of what can be done for the benefit of mankind just with money, I certainly would urge this government to do everything in their power to encourage the development of our vast resources, in order that they may be processed and exploited for the benefit of mankind. I am one of those who believe that we have a perfect right to exploit our natural resources for this day and generation, provided that we replace the replaceable resources so that those who are yet to come may enjoy some of the same advantages that we enjoy. But I believe that this government could give greater leadership and could inspire our people to greater heights.
When I think of the reference made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech to building up a surplus because of the unfor-

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny
tunate international situation which might lead to greater requirements for armed services, I think that is just about the poorest excuse for a surplus I ever heard of in my life; because we could not budget for enough, in anticipation of what might be before us, to maintain an army in the field for thirty days, if war ever breaks again; and God help us if it does. It will certainly be a war of survival, and it will take more than the present finance minister's budgets and surpluses and everything else to save mankind. The thing is to bring to our people some degree of relief at the present moment, and to budget so that they will throw off the shackles of burdensome taxation, exercise their God-given freedom, enjoy some degree of enthusiasm and develop their ambitions to provide this country with the productive capacity of which I know it is fully capable.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
With very much of what the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case) has just said, Mr. Speaker, I find myself in agreement. It is unfortunate that we do not hear more speeches of that character from my hon. friends to the right, and I shall have something to say about that a little later on.
One thing apparently that the public as a whole is agreed upon is this. There is general disappointment with the budget of 1948. Some of the newspapers have called it the "vinegar" budget, perhaps owing to the removal of the tax on spirits which go into vinegar. Others have called it the "black" budget. But it has been generally agreed that this budget has not been a satisfactory one so far as the people of Canada are concerned. What the reasons are for that I will not at this time enumerate, because they have been mentioned by others. We might perhaps look behind the scenes a bit and find out from where the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has been receiving advice in connection with fiscal policy. I have in my hand an exceTpt from a newsletter which is called the Letter Review, published by the Review Company of Fort Erie North, Ontario. It is dated February 9, 1948. This is a leaflet which comes through the mail to all members of the house and which, to my mind, is one of the most reactionary pieces of literature I ever saw. This is the advice which was handed out, and I quote it because it happens to coincide closely with the attitude of the finance minister:
Inflationary pressure, as it affects the price of the necessities of life, does not arise from excessive purchasing power on the part of the few, buit from excessive purchasing power in the hands of the masses.
So says this Letter Review. Then it goes on:
A government which proposes to use fiscal machinery for the relief of inflationary pressures has to start out by imposing unpopular taxation where it will hurt most, not by silly attempts to tax where it will hurt least.
The import of that, of course, is that the finance minister is being advised to tax the masses of the people, as they describe them, who have, in the opinion of the Letter Review, too much money to spend. Of course the figures given in this house yesterday evening by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) completely disprove that premise, because he proved in figures that the large majority of the people of this country do not have too much money to spend. It appears to me that the Minister of Finance has accepted that advice and has been using the fiscal policy of this country to extract still more money from the people in the lower income brackets rather than going for it where the money actually is. I should like to quote, too, an opinion as to the condition of affairs in this country by a person who. I think, will be accepted by the members of the Liberal party as somewhat of an authority on Liberal policy. I refer to Hon. Stuart Garson, Premier of Manitoba. This appears in a publication entitled The Canadian Liberal, and published under date of "Spring, 1948." I suppose it is a quarterly publication, and this is the most recent issue. In that journal Premier Garson has this to say about Canada:
. . . Canada today
(1)	has no national social security program;
(2)	has no national public investment program . . .
(4)	still has overlapping old age pensions administration;
(5)	still has overlapping three-way responsibility for relief, which in the depression of the 1930's was disastrous to the municipalities and the provinces;
(6)	still faces a complete lack of co-ordination in the efforts of ten different governments to combat any future depression communicated from the outside world.
Then this significant paragraph appears further on:
The enemies of our democracy could not devise an argument against it more persuasive than the conditions of governmental confusion and frustration in this country in the 1930's. Today free society is under sa'-age attack. Whv should we, by our inertia, reduce its defences?
Those words by the Premier of Manitoba are as strong as need be used to point out that again the government is following a policy of drift and laissez faire, and is making no plans whatever for the future. For this reason the members of the party with which
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny

I am associated decided to move an amendment. We now have before the house the amendment moved by the official opposition, which says in short that the government no longer has the confidence of the country. We * felt that was inadequate, because it is quite obvious that sitting in the opposition we would not have much confidence in the government ourselves, but we wanted to set out why we feel the government has not the confidence of the people as a whole.
So our amendment sets out what I think are constructive proposals, which may be summarized in these words. We suggest: first, that the government take action to raise the exemption levels for taxation purposes to $1,250 for single persons and $2,500 for married persons; second, that they remove or substantially reduce indirect or hidden taxes such as the sales tax and the excise tax, about which I shall have more to say later; third, that they launch a program of public investment designed to expand industry, particularly in western Canada, and channel investment into socially desirable fields such as the building of homes; fourth, that they balance and stabilize the Canadian economy by controlling prices of consumer goods and reducing the cost of production for Canadian agriculture. I believe those four proposals summarize what the people of Canada are today asking the government to do.
I need not take up more time in discussing the budget itself, because what I have already said and what has been said by the members of this group constitute our criticism of and also our alternatives to the budget proposals. The remainder of the time at my disposal I should like to devote to a reply to some of the statements which have been made by some members of the Progressive Conservative party, particularly the hon. member for Eglin-ton (Mr. Fleming), who spoke on May 24. I do this, not because I wish to approach this discussion in a spirit of political phlebotomy, but because the members of the Progressive Conservative party have gone out of their way within the last three or four days to criticize rather severely the C.C.F. and, I think more or less unfairly, to attack the C.C.F. party as being connected with some subversive forces in this country, or something of that sort. They have made statements which in my opinion must be answered; otherwise the country may get the impression that the statements are correct. What I have to say will be said in a kindly fashion, because I have many good friends to my right whom personally I like very much; but because I disagree with the opinions they have expressed and because I wish to correct their statements,

it will be necessary for me to refer to what they have said; and I hope they will take it in the spirit in which it is given.
The hon. member for Eglinton began by saying that the government is falling into line with the socialist philosophy, as he called it, of the managed economy. I shall quote directly from his speech, to be sure I do not misrepresent what he said. At page 4320 of Hansard he used these words:
This managed economy idea is of the essence of socialism. The socialists believe in the managed economy.
Let us have a word on this question of managed economy. You know the trouble with a great many slogans and catchwords is that when they go out, well trimmed up, they may sound quite evil and sinister, when actually they may be very innocent. In its essence, what is a managed economy? Surely even the hon. member for Eglinton would not get up in this house and argue for a mismanaged economy or one that is not managed at all. He would admit that management is necessary in the affairs of the country in much the same way that management is necessary in the affairs of our daily life. What he appears to object to, if I understand him correctly, is the government having any hand in managing the over-all affairs of the nation. Rather, it appears to me, he would favour allowing the so-called forces of free enterprise, supply and demand and so on, to act by themselves in a sort of vacuum, with checks and balances supplying the answer.
I suppose that is a perfectly sincere view, and he is entitled to it; but let me refer him to a statement I find in an interesting little book entitled "John Bracken Says", which was published in 1944, just before the election. The leader of the opposition, at that time not yet a member of this house, was discussing agriculture. It is quite true he did not use the words "managed economy", but this is what he did say; and before I read it I want to say that I agree with him. At page 132 he said:
What do I mean when I speak of guaranteeing the farmer against income fluctuation? I mean simply this: that the farmers, as a producing section of our population, shall receive their proportionate share of the national income of the country-a small income should the nation's income be small, and a proportionate share if it be large-a proportionate share, based on the number of people working on farms. That includes farm operators and farm workers.
How would anyone go about giving the farmers a proportionate share of the national income in an unmanaged economy? Surely, if the hon. member were going to carry out

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny
this promise and make it good to the Canadian farmers he would need to have some control over the affairs of the country, not only over the agricultural economy but over all the other things that enter into production on the farms. Then he continues, using that awful word "plan", and says:
The plan will, at the beginning, be applied to the more important farm products, and will be extended as rapidly as possible to cover the whole field of production in agriculture and other food products, including fish.
As I said before, I agree with the leader of the opposition that the agricultural population of the country is entitled to its fair proportion of the national income; but I do not see how anyone assuming power in this country could make good on that promise unless he were to assume a certain amount of control over the national economy. If the leader of the opposition ever did come to power I am sure one of the first things he would have to do in order to carry out this promise would be to repudiate the philosophy of the hon. member for Eglinton and those who agree with him.
I shall refer to that question again later on, but now I want to come to another matter. The hon. member for Eglinton and some other speakers to my right have been having a real field day talking about socialism, communism and matters of that kind, and have made quite an attempt to link up the communist party with the C.C.F., using, if you please, as an authority some statements by Tim Buck. It seems strange that they would use him as an authority when it suits their purpose, but will not believe him at any other time. I want to refer them to something, and I do so because it is so easy to make statements and attacks of this kind. Just because Tim Buck happened to say that in his opinion the communists should vote for a certain party, ipso jacto the hon. member for Eglinton takes that to be the gospel. I would not be so sure. I have here a clipping which dates back to about 1942, and which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press. It reports a meeting at Massey Hall, at which the leader of the communist party, Tim Buck, was present-this was at the time the communist party was banned'-* and the then premier of Ontario, Mr. Hepburn. Then, if you please, the third member on the platform with Mr. Buck was-well, let me quote from the clipping:
In addition to the premier and Mr. Buck, speakers included Leopold Macaulay, conservative member of the Ontario legislature for York South.
Incidentally the purpose of the meeting was to urge that the ban on the communist party
be lifted. Does this mean that Mr. Hepburn and Mr. Macaulay are communists?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What date was that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was 1942. Nor does it mean that the communist party was going to vote for these gentlemen at the next election, or vote for them in any other election, just because they happened to be on the same platform that night, I would not say so. They were there because they all agreed on something. Incidentally the C.C.F. did not have a man on the platform, apparently, while the other two parties had. But to attack the C.C.F. for things which are much more innocent than that is, in my view, unfair, and taking advantage of catchwords and slogans which do not add to any party's reputation.
While I am on the subject, I should like to refer to the answer made in the Windsor Star by Mr. Cameron, who made an extensive study and wrote articles on this question of communism, and the cure for communism. He said this:
There is no cure for communism because communism is not a disease; it is a symptom. It is an expression of the vast unrest that permeates all the people of the world not excepting our own, as the result of the moral, spiritual and economic breakdown of bourgeois capitalism.
That might give us something to think about. Instead of going around accusing each other of communism, I think we should go to work to erect a new structure to replace the breakdown of capitalism, go about it seriously, and be willing to co-operate with each other.
Hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party should realize that when they attack socialism and when they attack the system which now exists in Great Britain, New Zealand, Australia and some of the Scandinavian countries they are not doing any good to the world, that indeed they are doing it immeasurable harm. In all these areas the people have got together, and in a democratic way have elected governments which, in their opinion, are applying a correct policy. It is not adding to the good will of the world, or to the good will in any democratic country when people go out and attack a political system just because they happen to be in disagreement with it; and then link it up with communism or with any other old thing in order to smear it and blacken its name. I do not think it is good either for democracy, for progress or for any of the things which hon. members in this house profess to support.
I should like to quote briefly from some authorities who deal with this question of socialism and whom I would much rather
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitn y

accept than the spokesmen of the Progressive Conservative party, or anyone who believes the way they do.
For example, the late Archbishop of York, William Temple, said this:
The vast system of beliefs, practices and policies which may roughly be called western civilization . . . was admirably adapted to the production of wealth and power. But its motives were non-Christian, self-interest, competition, the struggle of rival forces. If it is to be a blessing, not a blight, its motives must be transformed.
There was a man who was not afraid of progress, who was not afraid to call a spade a spade. He saw the structure of the capitalist society going in the wrong direction, and said that its motives should be transformed- which is exactly what the C.C.F. is advocating.
Then we have the Papal Encyclical of 1931, in which Pope Pius XI said this:
You assuredly know and lament the ultimate consequences of this individualistic spirit in economic affairs. Free competition is dead; economic dictatorship has taken its place. Unbridled ambition for domination has taken its place. Unbridled ambition for domination has succeeded the desire for gain; the whole economic life has become hard, cruel and relentless in a ghastly measure.
It is rightly contended that certain forms of property must be reserved to the state since they carry with them an opportunity for domination too great to be left to private individuals without injury to the community at large.
I say again that here we have an expression of opinion from a disinterested party, one who is not interested in politics as such but who advises perhaps the largest single unit of faith on earth, that the system which we term capitalism, because of the results it has produced must be changed in certain respects, and he goes so far even, as to suggest certain fundamental changes. Surely we are not so small in this parliament as to oppose progress just because someone calls it socialism.
I wish it were possible for us to drop all the old slogans and all the old names, because I am sure we would be surprised at how much common ground we would find among ourselves. Hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party, such as the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) have risen in the house and advocated public ownership of public utilities such as telephone systems. Other members of the same party, perhaps in a disguised form, perhaps in a form which they themselves did not recognize, have advocated socialism in the house. In spite of the arguments they used against the Canadian wheat board, when the question
TMr. Zaplitny.]
was put to the house they voted for it. This is another method of doing something collectively which cannot be done individually. In other words, the whole membership of the House of Commons has been going toward what might be described as a socialistic system-and I hesitate to use the word because it antagonizes some hon. members. But actually what we are working toward is a system of co-operation. We are replacing the system of competition and rivalry and cutthroat business practice by a system of co-operation and doing collectively what cannot be done individually.
Call it what you like. We of the C.C.F. call it democratic socialism, and we are attacked for it. Other hon. members must realize they are advocating the same thing, only they have not attached the same name to it.
I come to a quotation from the Roman
Catholic hierarchy of Saskatchewan in 1934 which states:
It is abundantly clear why the church, condemns and abhors the abuses of the materialistic capitalism of our industrial age with its consequent unemployment for the masses and huge fortunes for the few. These evils are so well known that we are saved the trouble of listing them here. Suffice it to say that materialistic capitalism is so un-Christian in its philosophy and evi'l consequence that it must give way to a reconstructed social order based on Christian principles.
What language could be stronger than that? Again it comes from a source which does not take sides politically, but it is sincerely advising its people to be bold enough and to have the spirit of the pioneer to go out into new systems to see if they cannot improve their conditions.
Finally, from the United Church report of 1939 we find this as part of the report of the social service committee of that church:
We are driven to the conclusion that the only thing that will solve our present day social and economic problems will be the absolute Christian socialization of the means of production and distribution of all the necessities of life
There again we find the word "socialization" used. Immediately someone will say, "they mean that the government should take everything over and that everything should be state-owned". Of course it does not mean that. Socialization of the means of production and distribution does not necessarily involve state ownership, nor does it even necessarily involve public ownership in its various forms. But it means that the methods of production and distribution shall serve the ends of society as a- whole. That is why the word "socialization"

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny
is used. It means the socialization of the motive for which things are done. Instead of things being done for profit, the future motive should be to serve the public, the community, society as a whole.
With these authorities before us, surely no one in the house or elsewhere would seriously attack socialism. Whether they agree or do not agree with the methods which the C.C.F. would use to bring about a spirit of co-operation and good will, surely they cannot disagree that these principles are supported by the greatest spiritual and moral authorities on earth.
I go on to another term which has been bandied around, and that is paternalism. The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) said they were opposed to paternalism creeping into the affairs of this country. What is paternalism? The dictionary meaning of it is, anything done in a fatherly way. I do not know why anyone should object strenuously if the government wants to be a father, provided that it does not use the rod too often.
But for the Progressive Conservative party to object to paternalism would be funny if it were not so tragic. We know the history of the tariff structure in this country. We know it was a Conservative prime minister back in 1878 who started the first real tariff wall in this country which exists today, and which governments since then have continued in some modified form. In 1855 in this country we had reciprocity with the United States, which was ended in 1866 because of certain things done by Sir Alexander Galt in 1859. In 1878 Sir John A. Macdonald came out with what is called the national policy. In his opinion it was necessary to set up a tariff structure to prevent manufactured goods from coming into this country so that our own manufacturing industries could get a start.
That system has been extended in different forms. One government would bring the tariff down a little and another would raise it a little bit. Under the Bennett administration we had the highest tariff structure ever in this country. If that is not paternalism I should like to know what is.
How many members of the Progressive Conservative party would say they would favour the removal of all tariffs so far as Canada is concerned? The silence, Mr. Speaker, speaks for itself. There is not one. They are all in favour of paternalism when it comes to the protection of industry, and perhaps they have something there. But why should they attack the government or the C.C.F. because we wish to do something for the other people in this country? There again a term is used without much thought being given to its meaning.
I want to come a little closer and grapple with the question of the sales tax. The hon. member for Eglinton worked himself into quite a lather over the sales tax. He called it a plunder and other words which I do not wish to use because they were not well received by the Chair. What is the record? Why should the hon. member get so excited about it? The record is here. In 1930 the sales tax stood at one per cent. The Bennett administration came into power and in 1931 raised the sales tax to four per cent, and in 1932, to six per cent. In 1935 the Liberal administration came back and raised the sales tax to eight per cent in 1936. There is the history of the sales tax, pure and simple, for everyone to read.

Hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party may say they were not responsible for that, and they would be correct. But the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), speaking in this house on July 9, 1946, had this to say of the sales tax:
Very few of our people today know there is already a sales tax imposed at the wholesale level. Such a tax does not discourage the worker from working, and there is fairness in a tax policy based on the .principle that the more one spends, the more one pays.
I do not agree with him there. He went on:
There is nothing obligatory about paying a tax if one does not purchase.
It appears that the Progressive Conservatives have found a new solution for dodging the sales tax-stop buying. If you do not buy you do not pay the sales tax. But most of us are accustomed to eating and doing things of that sort.
I come now to another statement which I think is quite illuminating. The hon. member for Eglinton talked about social security. I agree with him that we have need of a comprehensive program of social security in this country. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), speaking in this house in 1946, said at page 1751 of Hansard of that year:
Leading economists tell us we shall have to increase our national income ... by fifty per cent if we are to maintain these new types of fantastic Liberal policies.

Apparently he was not satisfied with what we were doing because these social services cost too much. I remember vividly the present leader of the opposition rising in his place not very long ago and saying that billion dollar spending must stop. If we were to stop billion dollar spending there would be precious little left for social security. But while attacking the C.C.F., the Progressive Conservatives have forgotten their own record.
I come to something else which will be really interesting to the Progressive Conservative party. I have already pointed out certain contradictions in what they have suggested, but perhaps the crowning one is in what they have done rather in what they have said. In 1942 that party chose a new leader, and only that party could have chosen for its leader a man whom they had described only a few years before as a complete failure.

That is right. That is why he left Manitoba, to take the leadership of the Progressive Conservative party. Here is a document which is probably the only one of its kind in captivity. It starts out with a bold headline, "The Bracken Government Has Failed The Farmer!" It goes on to say:
The Conservative party has always claimed that under Mr. Bracken the farmer was getting a raw deal, but never expected Air. Bracken would admit it.
And further:
Fourteen years ago Air. Bracken and his party were elected on the promise to aid agriculture and reduce the cost of government.
Fourteen years later Air. Bracken, who has always claimed to be the friend of the farmer, admits that agriculture has not had a square deal; and admits he cannot reduce the cost of government.
It goes on:
What can you expect from Air. Bracken who in fourteen years has failed-[DOT]
Failed to do what? Failed:
To reduce the burden of your municipal taxes and municipal debt.
To reduce the interest burden on the provincial debt.
To reduce the cost of government.
That awful phrase again!
To provide hydro-electrical services to rural Manitoba 'at low- cost.
To ensure a fixed price for your wheat.
This is the first time I have heard criticism of a provincial premier for having failed to ensure a fixed price-a fixed price, of all things -by a party which does not believe in a managed economy! It goes on:
The Bracken government has penalized the wage earner and all people with small incomes.

He was then described as "Two per cent Bracken". It goes on:
The two per cent wage tax must be abolished. Cost of government must be reduced.
By whom was this published? It was published by the Conservative Association of Manitoba. Here was a glaring case of a party, after having completely destroyed the reputation of a man whom it had described as a complete failure to agriculture and the wage earners, then, with that characteristic contradiction of terms which they always use, electing him as leader of their party.

In rising to speak in this debate on the budget, if it is possible to call it a budget, I shall endeavour to -bring out a few facts and suggestions which I think will be of benefit to the gentleman who brings in the budget the next time. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) should have stayed as Minister of National Defence, because I am sure that anybody who would venture to bring in a budget to make so many people throughout Canada mad has a great nerve, and at the present time that is what is required of a Minister of Defence for Canada.
I am told that probably I am the last speaker in the debate, but I want it understood that I am not the least. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) referred to some remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) to the effect that the Liberals were following too much the tactics of the C.C.F. Well, we do not have to look back very far to find that the government have been exercising a lot of control, and, as I understand the tactics of the party to my left, they, too, exercise a lot of control in their own minds.
The only way in which I will attempt to answer the criticism, though I do not know that I should call it criticism, of the last speaker in regard to what he termed the Tory party-it is the Progressive Conservative party -is to say that we are very glad he is finding fault with us. I might also say that, call it democratic socialism, or C.C.F. or whatever you like, they are still after state control. The hon. gentleman who spoke last mentioned the communists. The communists also want state control. The only difference between those two parties is that, being both after

The Budget-Mr. A. E. Robinson
the same goal, they are jealous of each other. I may say, however, that in the provincial election in Ontario which is being held on June 7, Tim Buck and his followers are behind the C.C.F., and any remarks they make are along the line that if a C.C.F. government is elected in Ontario they will be giving them all the power of all their unmoral support which they are allowed to.

Yes. I may say for the benefit of hon. members from the west that a special train will leave Vancouver on July 15, arriving in Bruce on the opening day of its centennial. According to the last reports, that special train will carry three sections when leaving Winnipeg.
Bruce county has 300 miles of shoreline and most of that takes in what is called the Bruce peninsula. That peninsula has been spoken of before as a model site for a national park, and I see that this year we are budgeting for
$5,000,000 for national parks in Canada. I hope that the good people of that peninsula will see fit to have that district made into a national park and benefit to a certain extent from that $5,000,000.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the fishing is good.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Incidentally, the fishing is very good. The people in that county are looking forward to such a thing, because we have under reforestation over
12,000	acres of the district. We have also in Bruce a lot of good farming land. We are blessed with a good agricultural representative and assistants. Owing to the initiative of these representatives, we have tuberculosis testing in cattle under way, soil testing, warble fly control, barberry extermination, calf vaccination for Bang's disease and, as I have mentioned, reforestation, as well as fifteen calf clubs organized.
You can readily believe from what I have said, Mr. Speaker, that we have a wonderful county; nevertheless in the last seven years, the rural population has declined 3,385. This means that there are many empty houses in Bruce. It means that there is a good deal of land not producing to capacity for lack of help.
I charge this government with being responsible for these conditions. I charge the government with encouraging centralization over the last number of years. I can hardly see how the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) can expect ever to come back as a farmer member elected to the House of Commons in view of the record of the Liberal government so far as its treatment of farmers is concerned. The same applies to the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris) and the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding).
For the good of Canada, whatever government is in power, it must concentrate on ways and means to encourage decentralization both in population and in power. The government must give greater exemptions in income tax to farmers for the long hours of work which the farmer himself puts in and the work done by his wife and family.
Speaking of exemptions from income tax, I would also suggest that the government consider exemptions up to $3,000 for all men and women up to the age of thirty. This is something new and is worthy of consideration by the Minister of Finance. It is sound not only because I thought of it myself, but the more I think of it the more worthy I think it is of consideration. I repeat that there should be an exemption up to $3,000 for all

men and women up to the age of thirty. By this, all those young people will save money enough to marry and raise families. Today there are couples who are afraid to get married on the small amount they can save. In my opinion the increasing of population by this method would be much more satisfactory than spending large sums on immigration. It would also do away with a lot of the illegitimate baby scandals we read about in different parts of Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Second, earmark a good percentage of the taxes collected for temperance education in our schools. Third, lower the alcoholic content of our beer-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

To show that high prices do not curtail drinking, I wish to state that in 1893 when liquor was very cheap, the consumption of absolute alcohol per capita in Canada was 0-499 gallons; in 1945, with our high prices, the consumption was 0-630 gallons. These figures I have given might be larger if they were taken up to date. I may say that less liquor revenue would make all governments more interested in temperance education.
I wish to say just a few words about controls, from which we in Canada have suffered so much-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Birth control?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and from which we would suffer more if we had1 a C.C.F. government. I know that the C.C.F. group on my left will not agree, because they wish state control of everything, the same as the Labour Progressive or communist party want.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: More nonsense.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Speaking of controls, may I say that from June 1, 1947, to the end of that year, all dairy products were taken out from under control except cheese. During that period, all dairy products except cheese increased in production. Butter alone increased 17,000,000 pounds in that time, compared with production in the same period of the year before. If those controls had not been on dairy products, this house and the senate would not have been debating the margarine bill, and wasting our time in doing so, as we have been doing.
To come back to party politics, I wish to say that in Bruce we have a good active federation of agriculture, and also a few co-operatives. Some people would lead one to believe that both these lean toward the party to the left, the C.C.F., but I think I am safe in saying that in Bruce there is no such calamity hanging over our heads.

I should also like to see Canada enter into an extensive exchange of scholarships with every other nation in the world. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be quite willing to see a vote on the C.C.F. amendment tonight but for the fact that, once that amendment is out of the way, there will not be much left to talk about. I should not like to be placed in the position of having to vote on the straight, anaemic amendment moved by the Conservative party. It seemed to me that they did not have much to talk about, or much to propose, or any serious objections to the budget, when they merely presented a motion stating that the people of this country have no confidence in the government. I would not want to spend much time in this house, or stay too long in the vacuum in which I live here in Ottawa, trying to tell anyone that I know very much about what the people of this country are thinking. So I am taking these fifteen minutes tonight for the purpose of drawing attention to the amendment moved by this party, and the amendment moved by the Conservative party.
Whether we like it or not, the budget is a document which required careful preparation. It is a bookkeeping statement presented each year by the government in order to set out the financial picture of the country; and in order to criticize it I think one must have something to suggest in its place. At least one must have certain points that he can suggest to the government should be brought in, and I cannot see my way clear to support an amendment which merely states that the people of this country have no confidence in the present government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have you confidence?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not saying that, but I say I do not imagine the people of this country have any confidence in the people who proposed the amendment, either. I think that has been pretty clearly demonstrated all over this country. Go to British Columbia, Alberta. Saskatchewan or Nova Scotia; what

has happened there to the Conservative party? It has just disappeared. The remnants have their arms around the neck of the government and are holding themselves up as coalitionists.
A few minutes ago the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) threw something at the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) just after he sat down, after having referred to the coalitions in force all over Canada today between the Conservatives and the Liberals, who are trying to hang on to the old, worn-out system. The hon. member for Vancouver North rose and asked, "Well, is that any worse than the coalition which exists between the CC.F. and the communist party?" The hon. member for Dauphin was not permitted to reply, but the answer is this. I do not blame the hon. member for Vancouver North for being allergic to the situation out in British Columbia. From what I can gather through the grapevine, he expects to inherit the mess out there. He may have to lead the government there some time; and what a position to place a Liberal in, to sit him on the government benches with the remnants of the Tory party and have, to make a deal with them as to the kind of legislation that should be passed! So that accounts for the suggestion he threw out, which he knows is absolutely incorrect, because in this house the' hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and others have clearly stated the position of the C.C.F. with respect to the communist party.
Now I think we have had enough of that sort of thing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think so.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not blame you fellows for being jittery about that sort of subject, because you are very vulnerable. I would suggest that some of you older members brief the younger ones and tell them not to stick out their necks so often.
I want now to get around to the budget. As I said before, it required a great deal of preparation; and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made a very good job of presenting it to the house. He was convinced, I think, that he was right. This afternoon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), who had the job of looking after the Department of Finance all through the war, also did a good job. He made an excellent speech, and I am sorry that so far he is the only maritime member to have taken part in this debate. But I should like to say to my hon. friends over here to the extreme right that the Minister of Finance, charged with the responsibility of

The Budget-Mr. Gillis
doing his bookkeeping and keeping the country's financial set-up in balance under the mechanics of the society in which we live, did it in the only way open to him.
This afternoon the Minister of Justice made an excellent speech in support of a continuation of the status quo. He could not make any other kind of speech and be a private enterpriser. But I cannot understand how the hon. member over here in the Tory party who is supposed to be a better private enterpriser than any Liberal, can get up and object to the kind of statement brought down by the Minister of Finance or to the kind of speech made by the Minister of Justice this afternoon. I am giving those hon. gentlemen credit for supporting the mechanics of the society in which they believe; and I am only glad that this gang over here are not over there, because I know the budget would have been much worse. This business of saying, "We believe the people of this country no longer have confidence in the government," and Stopping there shows clearly, as the speeches they have made show clearly, that there is very little in this budget with which they can quarrel. They quibble about it, but there has not been any constructive objection in opposition to it, and the amendment certainly-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are listening to you.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you will hear something before I have finished. I am only fooling with you yet.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For sure?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And I will have thirty-five minutes of this tomorrow afternoon. The Progressive Conservative party has offered an amendment of only four lines to this 56-page document, an amendment which says that the people of this country have no confidence in the government. I speak tonight because I would not be able to speak on our amendment, had it gone to a vote tonight.
For the benefit of hon. members over here, I am going to read our amendment, because I am reasonably sure that most of them have not read it. And those who did hear it when it was moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar I am reasonably sure have forgotten it. Let me point this out, that I have heard a good deal of talk today about the low-income group, and that sort of stuff, which is pretty good political capital in this country. But if you will read our amendment, you will find that it says this:
That the said amendment be amended by inserting after the word "government" and before the word "does" in the second line of the 5849-282
amendment, the following words:	". . . has
failed to relieve the excessive burden of taxation on the low-income groups of the Canadian people:
(a)	By failing to increase the amouuts of exemption from income tax from the present levels to $1,250 for single and $2,500 for married persons, and
(b)	By failing to remove or substantially reduce the burden of sales and excise taxes which bear most heavily on those suffering from low income and the present high cost of living.
And further, the government has failed to establish a public investment board to assure the channelling of capital investment into socially desirable projects as a means of maintaining full employment, increasing production and raising the standard of living of the Canadian people, and . .
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) and other hon. members over here whom I have heard speak have picked on these very items-not the last one, of course-but on low-income groups, the sales tax and the excise tax. Why did they not include these things in their amendment? Why did they not ask for an amendment to the motion to adopt the budget by writing in specifically the things they believe the government has not done? That is one reason I say the official opposition should withdraw the amendment and get it out of the way. It is that trick of just a nonconfidence motion with nothing behind it- it is so old that it has whiskers on it. There is no solution there. Why not just withdraw it and allow the subamendment to be the main amendment? Then hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party could stand behind the things they have said in the House of Commons-those few of them who have expressed any real opinions in regard to the budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Get down to business.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is just a little advice I am giving my hon. friends. Let us try to get some clarification into this thing. Let us realize we are discussing a document that has a lot of meat in it. Let us write clearly into the amendment the things the government should have done and has not done. Then let us stand up here and be counted as to where we stand with respect to those points the government did not introduce.
With respect to relief for low-income groups, I have heard the statement made on several occasions by the Minister of Finance that the income tax in Canada is much lower than in the United States, and he placed on record in that connection a table showing the tax for unmarried persons in the country. That
The Budget-Mr. Gillis

table does not coincide with a table I have. I believe the one I have is reliable, because it comes from the Financial Post of April 17, 1948. This table gives the 1948 rates of taxation for a married man with two children, and gives a comparison of Canadian and United States rates. The table states that in the category I have mentioned the taxpayer in Canada pays $36, while in the same category in the United States he pays no tax. I am referring to the $2,000 bracket. Then, in the $4,000 bracket in Canada there is a tax of $430 and in the United States a tax of only $266. This is for a married man with two children. Then, for the $10,000 group the tax in Canada is $1,930, while in the United States it is $1,361. The same ratio carries right through to $25,000.
So that the argument that taxes are much lower in Canada than in the United States does not hold, if the table set out in this issue of the Financial Post is correct.
On motion of Mr. Gillis the debate was adjourned.
